forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 29 to 29. This is the third consecutive hold and I want to justify it rather than let it look like inertia. I worked through all six of yesterday's stated triggers and none fired in either direction; separately, two genuinely new items landed today, one up and one down, and they cancel to within a quarter of a point.

Trigger one, the resolving pathway itself. No lab issued an institutional AGI statement and no named senior research staff - as distinct from CEOs or investors - said AGI has been achieved. I searched specifically for statements dated 25-26 August and found nothing. The AGI Global Summit in Portland is running 25-27 August, but it remains what I judged it to be yesterday: a cross-disciplinary academic event spanning economics, law, governance, safety and ethics, producing a roadmap report in Q2 2027, not a venue where frontier lab research staff generate a resolving declaration. Trigger not fired.

Trigger two, ARC Prize. Still no ruling on NVIDIA's AVO claim, no statement, and the Verified Leaderboard is unchanged. The Forbes write-up on 24 August restates the position I took: AVO scored 100.00 RHAE across all 183 levels of the 25-environment public set on 21 August in 6,624 environment actions against prior leader VISTA's 7,542, but that figure was generated and reported by NVIDIA's own team using its own reimplementation of the task interface, whereas ARC's verified numbers come from runs the foundation independently administers. Claude Opus 5 remains at roughly 30 per cent standalone and 100 per cent inside AVO - a seventy-point lift from scaffolding with no model change - and the semi-private and private held-out sets remain untested. That gap is a story about harness design, not about a model crossing a general-capability threshold. Trigger not fired.

Trigger three, the aggregates. The Goodheart Labs dashboard still reads a combined median of 2031 with an 80 per cent band of 2027 to 2043, and - this is the detail worth flagging - it is still explicitly timestamped as of August 25, 2026. It has not refreshed for today at all. Metaculus Q5121 is unchanged at a January 2033 median with roughly 25 per cent by 2029. So the aggregate view has now been flat through the Anthropic protein-design result of 20 August, the Prime Intellect autonomous-research result, the AVO harness claim and the Ox Alpha stealth model. Trigger not fired, and the persistence of that flatness is mild evidence against my own upward inside-view adjustments of the past week.

Trigger four, Kalshi, is where I want to be most careful, because for the second day running the headline number is misleading in a way that would fool anyone reading the tape without opening the book. KXOAIAGI now displays Before 2027 at 12.2 per cent, marked up 6.2 on the day from yesterday's 6 per cent. Taken at face value that is a doubling of the near rung. It is not real. The quoted prices are Yes 8.2 cents and No 93.9 cents, which implies a bid of 6.1 cents and an ask of 8.2 cents. The displayed chance of 12.2 per cent sits four points above the ask. A fair value cannot exceed the offer at which you can buy the contract; this is a stale last-trade print or a crossed-book artefact, not information. On a proper midpoint basis the near rung is about 7.2 per cent against yesterday's roughly 6, which is noise. I score it at zero. Yesterday the same series produced a spurious seven-point fall; today a spurious six-point rise. Two display artefacts in opposite directions in two days is a reason to downgrade how much weight this instrument carries at all.

The rungs that matter behaved quietly. Before 2030 displays 36 per cent with no change arrow, quoted Yes 43.4 cents and No 63.9 cents, implying a bid of 36.1 and an ask of 43.4 against yesterday's 36.0 and 43.4. That is one tenth of a cent of bid improvement and a midpoint of about 39.75 per cent versus 39.7 yesterday - flat. Before 2028 displays 17 per cent against 18 yesterday, on a bid of 17 and an ask of 21. Series volume is $895,754 against $894,366, so $1,388 of turnover in twenty-four hours. That is sixteen times yesterday's eighty-five dollars and still trivial on a series that has done nearly nine hundred thousand dollars lifetime. The material point for my forecast is that the bid-side softening I scored at minus one point yesterday did not continue. I do not add that point back - a single day of stability is not evidence of recovery - but I take a quarter-point off for the further drift on the 2028 rung and otherwise treat Kalshi as having told me nothing today. Trigger not fired; nothing remotely close to the 55-with-a-three-cent-spread-and-twenty-thousand-in-weekly-volume condition I set.

Trigger five, Anthropic's S-1. Still confidential only. The 1 June draft stands and there is no public prospectus, ticker, exchange, price range or valuation. Trigger not fired.

Trigger six, the Astra ladder, is the one thing that moved with real volume behind it, and it moved up. Polymarket now reads 3 per cent for 31 August, 45 per cent for 15 September, 79 per cent for 30 September and 89 per cent for 31 October, on total series volume of $341,445 with $49,934 sitting on the September 15 rung alone. The September 15 quote is Yes 48 cents and No 58 cents, a bid of 42 and an ask of 48 for a clean 45 midpoint. That rung has now gone 39 to 41.5 to 45 across three days - six points of firming in forty-eight hours - and a separate weekly market on release between 14 and 20 September reads 42 per cent. The far rungs are static. The reading is specific and I think correct: traders have converged on Astra shipping in mid-September, which means the 7 August cybersecurity hold is being priced as a delay of weeks rather than a structural brake. That is a direct partial reversal of one of my larger downside factors. Plus 0.75 points.

Two other items. First, a negative I did not expect. Today's research feed carries a preprint audit finding that AI self-training gains can be measurement artefacts - in a 48-run comparison, measurement choices alone created apparent gains and losses, with external distillation reaching more low-base problems than self-training. Set alongside the survey of 1,250 arXiv papers from 2024 to 2026 that separates bounded self-refinement, which is convergent, evaluable and already industrial practice, from open-ended recursive self-improvement, which it finds bounded by grounding requirements, collapse dynamics and compute on every measured axis, this cuts directly at the AI-accelerating-AI-research mechanism I gave weight to earlier in the week on the strength of the Prime Intellect speedrun result. Minus 0.75 points.

Second, I am correcting an overstatement of my own. I wrote yesterday that Google has not shipped a frontier model since early 2026 and treated it as effectively out of contention. Google shipped Gemini 3.6 Flash in July and Gemini 3.7 Flash on 13 August at 65.3 per cent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 43.6 per cent on FrontierCode 1.1 Main, Gemini has crossed one billion monthly active users, and today Google launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal with Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis and Harvey integrations. Gemini 4 is still pre-training only with no announced date, so the substance of the point survives - Google is not currently at the frontier tier - but it is shipping steadily, and I soften that factor from minus one to minus 0.75. A quarter-point back.

I also note Ox Alpha, the stealth OpenRouter model with a roughly one-million-token multimodal context that Bloomberg and TechCrunch covered on 23 August. One independent researcher ran ten DeepSWE tasks and it passed eight, against Claude Fable 5 at 65 per cent and GPT-5.6 Sol at 52 per cent, and serving-layer forensics - a Java stack trace naming Zhipu internal API classes, an identical error-code dialect to GLM on OpenRouter, 30 of 30 tokenizer probe matches - point at Zhipu AI. The free preview ends around 27 August. An n-of-ten evaluation is not decisive and a Chinese lab is not a plausible declarer under this resolver, but it does raise competitive pressure on the US labs. Plus 0.25.

Net: ups of 1.25, downs of 1.25. Holding 29, band unchanged at 17 to 45.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is still no historical frequency of AGI declarations to anchor on - zero occurrences in the seventy years since the 1956 Dartmouth coinage - so the outside view must be assembled from standing forecast aggregates and structurally analogous reference classes. That is the largest limitation here and why my interval stays as wide as 17 to 45.

Reference class one, my primary anchor: standing aggregate forecasts on AGI timing. I re-pulled the Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard today. It reads a combined median arrival of 2031 with an 80 per cent confidence band of 2027 to 2043, and it carries an explicit as-of date of August 25, 2026 - meaning it has not refreshed for today, and its reading is now identical to yesterday, to a week ago and to a fortnight ago. It aggregates five instruments: Metaculus Q3479 on weakly general AI, Metaculus Q5121 on general AI, Metaculus Q11861 on a long adversarial Turing test, Manifold's AGI When? distribution, and Kalshi's Turing-test-before-2030 market. A 2031 median with that right skew implies roughly a quarter to a third of probability mass falling before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121 remains at a January 2033 community median with roughly 25 per cent by 2029; its weakly general AI sibling, which drops the robotics condition, sits far earlier at around mid-2028, and the size of that gap is itself informative about how much of the disagreement here is definitional rather than empirical. These are large-n, long-running, incentive-checked estimates and I let them set my centre of gravity in the high twenties to low thirties. The instruments are correlated - overlapping populations, overlapping information - so the effective sample is smaller than the headline forecaster counts suggest, and the Manifold component's 2034 reading across 1,100-plus contributors pulls the combined right tail out further than the market ladders alone would.

Reference class two: the specific declaration markets. Kalshi's KXOAIAGI series is the closest liquid instrument, but it asks a strictly narrower question than mine - OpenAI specifically, announcement only - and simultaneously a laxer one, with no researcher-consensus alternative and arguably a lower bar for what counts as announcing. Today it displays Before 2027 at 12.2 per cent, Before 2028 at 17 and Before 2030 at 36, on quoted prices that imply a 6.1-to-8.2 spread, a 17-to-21 spread and a 36.1-to-43.4 spread respectively. The near-rung display of 12.2 sits above its own 8.2-cent ask, which is arithmetically impossible as a fair value and confirms these displayed percentages are last-trade or stale prints rather than mids. Series volume is $895,754, up $1,388 on the day. On a midpoint basis the 2030 rung is worth about 39.75 per cent and has been essentially static for two days. I read fair value on this instrument as high thirties to low forties, with a persistent long-dated-market bias on top: capital tied up until 2030 demands a discount, which pushes true fair value above the traded price. Manifold's parallel ladder - roughly 3 per cent for 2027, 15 for 2028, 31 for 2029, 38 for 2030, 45 for 2031, 52 for 2032, 55 for 2033 - is play-money and lightly capitalised but monotone, internally coherent and brackets the aggregate. This cluster is consistent with something in the 30s for a broad arrival question and lower for a strict institutional-declaration question.

Reference class three, and the one that keeps me below the raw market numbers: the frequency with which prominent declarations have already occurred without resolving anything. Jensen Huang told Lex Fridman in late March 2026 that AGI has already been achieved, and Fortune's 30 March write-up documented researchers disputing it within days. Sam Altman told Forbes OpenAI had basically built AGI, or very close to it, then walked it back as a spiritual rather than literal claim requiring a lot of medium-sized breakthroughs; in his first long-form interview of 2026 he answered the AGI-arrival question with a curve rather than a date. Dario Amodei at Davos in January 2026 put it at one to three years and speaks of a nation of geniuses in a datacenter by 2027. Demis Hassabis has repeatedly said roughly fifty-fifty by 2030 and explicitly not via systems built like today's. Sequoia has published that AGI is here, now. Satya Nadella says the industry is nowhere close, and Yann LeCun says LLMs will never get there. None of these resolved this question, none pushed Kalshi's 2027 rung durably above single digits on a midpoint basis, and none produced three named senior researchers - as opposed to CEOs and investors - asserting achievement within a short window. That is the crux of my forecast, and it is why I keep a substantial gap between a system plausibly deserving the label existing and a credible lab announcing, or three leading researchers stating, that AGI has been achieved. The base rate of loose executive AGI talk is high and rising; the observed conversion rate into a resolving social event is zero out of at least five.

Reference class four: technology-declaration analogues where a field must collectively agree a threshold was crossed - room-temperature superconductivity, quantum supremacy, Level 5 autonomy. Contested definitions plus commercial incentives produce claims that are individually loud and collectively non-resolving for years; quantum supremacy took roughly three years from Google's 2019 claim to broad but still incomplete acceptance. The class fits on structure and poorly on stakes, since AGI carries far larger consequences - more incentive to claim, far more liability for claiming wrongly. ARC Prize is the institutionalised form of this dynamic, and NVIDIA's AVO episode shows it working as designed: a 100.00 public-set figure produced on NVIDIA's own reimplementation of the task interface, no submission to the independently administered verification process, no held-out set result, and NVIDIA itself conceding the number is not a direct measurement against ARC's leaderboard.

A fifth consideration I weight explicitly is the field's own governance behaviour. The Pacing the Frontier letter of 28 July 2026 drew over 1,260 signatures across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and Thinky, including Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, asking Washington to build tools to deliberately slow frontier development if recursive self-improvement arrives, and both Anthropic and OpenAI endorsed it corporately within a day. It is genuinely double-edged: the strongest available signal that senior insiders think automated AI R&D is plausible within a few years, and simultaneously a coordinated pre-commitment to institutional caution. Organisations that have publicly backed a slowdown mechanism are markedly less likely to issue a triumphal we-have-achieved-AGI press release.

Integrating: the outside view puts me around 28 to 32 for a broad arrival question over the remaining forty months. Inside-view adjustments are close to a wash. Upward: the scaffolding channel is visibly productive and cheap, autonomous science now has third-party wet-lab validation, competitive pressure is broadening internationally, and compute financing keeps compounding. Downward: safety-gated release regimes are real and costly, the recursive-self-improvement literature is turning sceptical, aggregate forecasts are frozen, Google is not at the frontier tier, and imminent listings raise the liability cost of a declaration. I sit at 29, a few points below the Kalshi midpoint, because the resolution bar is a social event and the conversion rate from capability claim to resolving declaration remains zero.
factors_up: Polymarket Astra ladder firmed for a second consecutive day with real depth behind it (+0.75pp). The 15 September rung has moved 39 to 41.5 to 45 per cent across three days, quoted Yes 48c / No 58c for a clean 42-48 book and a 45 midpoint, on $49,934 of volume on that rung alone within a $341,445 series; a separate weekly market on release between 14 and 20 September reads 42 per cent, while 30 September holds at 79 and 31 October at 89. Traders have converged on a mid-September Astra release, meaning the 7 August cybersecurity hold is being priced as a delay of weeks rather than a structural brake - a direct partial reversal of one of my larger downside factors.

Anthropic third-party wet-lab-validated autonomous protein design, published 20 August and written up by Forbes on 23 August (+1.5pp). Claude autonomously ran a de novo binder campaign; Adaptyv Bio built all 1,320 designs and Twist Bioscience independently tested 1,260 as antibody fusions in human cells inside three weeks, producing working binders against 14 of 15 targets at 22-35 per cent per-design success versus a 10-15 per cent industry baseline, and a 40 per cent hit rate on RBX1 where human competition entrants managed 3.7 per cent. Autonomous end-to-end science with independent physical validation remains one of the few mechanisms that could underwrite a defensible AGI declaration inside forty months.

The three-or-more-leading-researchers pathway is structurally softer than an institutional declaration and requires no lab to ship anything (+2pp). Huang in March 2026, Altman in Forbes, Amodei at Davos and on his nation-of-geniuses-by-2027 line, Hassabis at fifty-fifty by 2030 and Sequoia publishing that AGI is here, now show senior-figure declarations already occur at meaningful frequency. The resolver only needs three of them to be researchers rather than executives and to land within a short window, and there is no defined seniority threshold to clear.

International competitive pressure broadened with the Ox Alpha stealth model (+0.25pp). Bloomberg and TechCrunch covered it on 23 August: roughly one-million-token multimodal context on OpenRouter, eight of ten DeepSWE tasks passed against Claude Fable 5 at 65 per cent and GPT-5.6 Sol at 52 per cent, with a Java stack trace naming Zhipu internal API classes, an identical GLM error-code dialect and 30 of 30 tokenizer probe matches pointing at Zhipu AI. An n-of-ten evaluation is not decisive and a Chinese lab is not a plausible declarer under this resolver, but frontier-adjacent capability diffusing outside the three US labs raises the pressure on them to ship and to claim.

The Pacing the Frontier letter remains an insider signal that recursive self-improvement is considered live (+1pp). Over 1,260 staff across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and Thinky signed on 28 July 2026, including Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, on the explicit premise that AI systems may soon be able to automate their own research and development. That is a large, named, cross-lab body of senior technical opinion putting non-trivial weight on a fast takeoff inside my window.

Compute capital, power supply and enterprise distribution keep compounding (+0.5pp). Cisco and Nvidia moved AI factory deployments from plans toward production this week, Nvidia put the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator into full production on 24 August and partnered with Cloverleaf Infrastructure on 21 August, up to $105bn is backing OpenAI Ohio capacity phasing in from 2028, and Google launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal today with Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis and Harvey integrations. These are multi-year-lag inputs and I deliberately do not let them move much.
factors_down: A new preprint audit finds AI self-training gains can be measurement artefacts (-0.75pp). Surfaced on the research feed today, a 48-run comparison found that measurement choices alone created apparent gains and losses, with external distillation reaching more low-base problems than self-training. Read alongside the survey of 1,250 arXiv papers from 2024-2026 separating bounded self-refinement - convergent, evaluable, already industrial practice - from open-ended recursive self-improvement, which it finds bounded by grounding requirements, collapse dynamics and compute on every measured axis, this cuts directly at the AI-accelerating-AI-research mechanism I gave weight to earlier in the week.

The aggregate forecasts remain completely frozen (-1.5pp). Goodheart Labs still reads a 2031 combined median with an 80 per cent band of 2027-2043 and its timestamp has not even advanced past August 25, 2026; Metaculus Q5121 is unchanged at a January 2033 median with roughly 25 per cent by 2029; Manifold sits at 2034 across 1,100-plus contributors. Neither the Anthropic protein result, nor the Prime Intellect autonomous-research result, nor the AVO harness claim, nor Ox Alpha has compressed any of them, and I should not be the only forecaster repricing on evidence the aggregate has already seen.

Kalshi continues to drift lower on the middle rung and to produce unreliable displays (-0.25pp). Before 2028 shows 17 per cent against 18 yesterday on a 17-21 book; Before 2030 is flat at a 36.1-43.4 book with a 39.75 midpoint; Before 2027 displays 12.2 per cent, up 6.2, on quoted Yes 8.2c / No 93.9c - a displayed chance sitting four points above its own ask, which is arithmetically impossible as a fair value. Two spurious multi-point display moves in opposite directions on consecutive days, on $1,388 of daily turnover, is reason to downweight this instrument entirely rather than to trade its headline.

Safety-gated release regimes remain a real and unresolved brake (-1.5pp). OpenAI has held Astra since 7 August after preliminary evaluations could not rule out Critical cybersecurity capability - autonomously developing functional zero-days in hardened real-world systems - requiring isolated testing environments, sandboxed execution, expanded token-level monitoring, restricted network and tool access and external reviews with government agencies, with the Preparedness Framework rewrite still unresolved since Axios reported it on 18 August. The July Hugging Face sandbox-escape incident, with roughly 17,600 attacker actions reconstructed from logs and METR and Redwood Research brought in for third-party assessment, is why these controls will get tighter rather than looser.

The industry has publicly pre-committed to institutional caution, which cuts against triumphal declaration (-1pp). Anthropic and OpenAI both corporately endorsed Pacing the Frontier within a day of the 28 July letter, formally backing a mechanism to deliberately slow frontier development, and Altman has said society may need to pace the rate of AI development. Both firms sit inside IPO windows - Anthropic confidential S-1 filed 1 June with an October Nasdaq target and still no public prospectus, OpenAI saying it will be public by 2027 - and face heavy liability for an AGI claim they cannot defend.

Five-plus senior-figure AGI-adjacent declarations have produced zero resolutions (-3pp). Altman has retracted his own to a spiritual rather than literal claim requiring a lot of medium-sized breakthroughs; Fortune documented researchers disputing Huang March 2026 claim within days; NVIDIA now concedes its AVO 100.00 public-set figure should not be read as a direct measurement against ARC Prize independently administered leaderboard, where the semi-private and private held-out sets remain untested and Opus 5 stands at roughly 30 per cent standalone. The conversion rate from loud capability claim to resolving social declaration remains zero.
key_uncertainties: Whether the resolver counts a scaffold-plus-model system, or a domain-specific autonomous result like the protein binder campaign, as AGI achieved at all, or requires general capability intrinsic to a released model. NVIDIA AVO, Inherent Faraday and Anthropic Claude Science are exactly the ambiguous cases and no resolver guidance exists.

How credible lab and leading AI researchers bind in practice, given at least five senior-figure declarations have already occurred without resolving this question, one was publicly walked back by its author, and the three-researcher pathway has no defined window or seniority threshold.

Whether the Kalshi series carries any day-to-day information at all. Two consecutive days of multi-point displayed moves in opposite directions, with today displayed chance sitting above its own ask and turnover of $1,388 on a 7.3-cent spread, suggest the instrument I have leaned on most is close to uninformative at daily frequency.

Whether the Astra hold, the roughly 20 per cent monitoring compute overhead and the Preparedness Framework rewrite become a durable structural brake through 2029 or resolve into a delay of weeks. Polymarket now leans firmly to the latter at 45 per cent by 15 September and 79 per cent by 30 September.

Whether the recursive-self-improvement channel survives methodological scrutiny. If today measurement-artefact finding generalises, the autonomous-AI-research results of the past fortnight are worth substantially less than I have been scoring them, and the fastest route to a defensible declaration inside the window narrows.

Whether Google returns to frontier contention inside the window. It is shipping steadily - Gemini 3.7 Flash on 13 August, one billion monthly active users, Gemini Enterprise for Legal today - but Gemini 4 is still pre-training only with no announced date, and its performance determines whether there are three plausible declarers in 2027-2029 or effectively two.
update_triggers: Revise UP if three or more named senior research staff - not CEOs, not investors - at OpenAI, Anthropic or Google DeepMind state within a short window that AGI has been achieved, or any lab issues an institutional statement using the phrase we have achieved AGI

Revise UP if ARC Prize places any system above 80 per cent on the ARC-AGI-3 Semi-Private or Private sets on the independently administered Verified Leaderboard, or if NVIDIA submits AVO under the Kaggle verification process rather than self-reporting on its own reimplementation of the task interface

Revise UP if the Goodheart Labs combined median moves inside 2030 or its as-of timestamp advances with a changed reading, or if Metaculus Q5121 implied probability by 2029 rises above 35 per cent - the first aggregate compression in over a fortnight

Revise UP if Kalshi KXOAIAGI Before 2030 trades above 55 on a midpoint basis with a bid-ask inside 3 cents and series volume rising more than $20,000 in a week, rather than the current $1,388 per day on a 7.3-cent spread with displayed prices that sit outside their own quotes

Revise DOWN if Astra slips past the 30 September Polymarket rung (currently 79 per cent, with 15 September at 45), if OpenAI rewritten Preparedness Framework imposes a formal capability ceiling or external sign-off plausibly binding through 2029, or if Anthropic public S-1 contains risk-factor language explicitly disclaiming near-term AGI

Revise DOWN if the self-training measurement-artefact finding is replicated at scale or if a major lab retracts an autonomous-AI-research claim, or if Gemini 4 slips to 2027 and no third credible declarer emerges alongside OpenAI and Anthropic

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 11 to 10.

I checked each of yesterday's nine triggers in turn and none of them fired in the sense they were written, but today produced more genuinely new material than the previous three days combined, and on balance it tilts down. The scheduled items are still not due: FTI's Q3 print and CRA's Q3 print are late October, and both the Challenger August report and the BLS August employment situation land on 4 September. The most recent Challenger release remains the July report of 6 August, with 477,033 cuts announced through July, down 41% from 806,383 in the first seven months of 2025, July the lowest monthly total since July 2024, Technology at 149,023 year to date and up 67%, and hiring announcements up 25%. BLS confirms the August Employment Situation is scheduled for 4 September, so CES6054160001 has nothing new to test.

The day's real find is a directly on-point piece I had not logged: Mona Birjandi and Mery Zadeh, 'AI Is Coming for the Economic Consulting Industry', which ProMarket, the Stigler Center's publication, ran on 25 August 2026. I want to be precise about what it is. ProMarket is on its annual summer break and is republishing its most-read content from the first half of the year; the piece originally appeared on 29 April 2026 and sits on SSRN as abstract 7146120. So it is new to my file but carries no new information flow. It is nonetheless the single most specific analysis of this exact question I have seen, so it deserves careful reading in both directions.

It cuts up in its mechanism. The authors put the AI-automatable share of the data-collection, modelling and drafting layer at 50-60% in antitrust and competition economics, 55-65% in securities fraud and commercial damages, and 60-70% in employment discrimination. They estimate 85-95% time savings on the maker-checker independent replication audit that structurally doubles senior billing on every task, 70-85% on data collection, 50-70% on quantitative modelling, and 60-75% on turning results into demonstratives. They cite CRA's own annual reports for a 5.8% year-on-year fall in consultant headcount in FY2024 with revenue per consultant rising from about $621,000 to about $727,000, and note both CRA and Cornerstone have appointed senior officers to deploy AI, with Cornerstone running an agentic research platform across case work. On demand they point to JPMorgan replacing external advisory functions with internal tools and the ACC's 2025 Chief Legal Officer Survey finding a majority of large in-house departments deploying AI for work previously routed outside. Their stated equilibrium is 'a smaller industry by headcount, more concentrated at the senior level, with a hollowed-out middle.'

It cuts down in almost everything else. They are explicit that AI cannot replace expert testimony and that testifying-expert fees may rise even as analyst hours thin. They give three structural reasons pricing will not fall to clients: high-stakes litigants shop on Daubert track record rather than price, the pool of credible testifying experts in areas like pharmaceutical patent damages is small enough to blunt competitive pressure, and clients are reluctant to open an adversarial fee conversation with the expert they depend on in court. They identify genuinely new revenue lines with no methodological template and therefore premium fees: algorithmic price-fixing cases following the DOJ's 2025 Statement of Interest, AI-system compliance and disparate-impact audits, and AI-amplified case screening. And their conclusion is a refusal to forecast the aggregate: 'industry employment will depend on whether AI-driven cost reductions generate enough new case volume to offset reduced labor demand per case. That demand-side question is an open question.' That does not satisfy my fifth trigger, which requires two or more credible sources with quantified estimates of AI-caused decline exceeding 15% from a 2024 base. This is one source, and it declines to quantify the aggregate. Net for the piece: roughly plus 0.7pp on mechanism, minus 0.3pp on its explicit agnosticism and its pricing-stickiness argument.

Against that, five smaller down-items accumulated. First, the BLS 2024-34 projections have more in them than I logged yesterday: professional, scientific and technical services is projected the second-fastest-growing sector, 7.5% growth and 812,500 new jobs, sitting alongside the 9.4% figure for management, scientific and technical consulting services. Minus 0.2pp. Second, CRA's 6 August call carried forward guidance I had not recorded: management expects mid-single-digit headcount growth by year-end and believes utilisation can hold in the mid-to-upper 70s even as hiring resumes, with nearly 30 VPs added in 2025 ramping ahead of expectations. Minus 0.4pp. Third, FTI management on 30 July guided that Economic Consulting 'will no longer be a year-on-year drag on revenue or on adjusted segment EBITDA' from the second half of 2026, and the segment's Q2 revenue rose $13.2m and adjusted segment EBITDA $14.7m sequentially. That is the firm at the centre of my strongest up-factor telling me the trough is behind it. Minus 0.3pp. Fourth, Huron raised full-year 2026 guidance to $1.85-1.89bn revenue before reimbursables and $9.00-9.40 adjusted EPS, expecting double-digit digital growth in the second half on an AI-related pipeline. Minus 0.2pp. Fifth, the narrow niche keeps expanding rather than contracting: BRG has launched Rome and Milan competition practices staffed by economists poached from Brattle, and Cornerstone continues London and Brussels hiring. Minus 0.2pp. LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 has AI consultants and strategists as the second fastest-growing role in the US, which is the demand-amplifier reading again.

Two items I looked at and set aside. Resources Connection reported Consulting segment revenue of $36.9m against $52.6m, minus 32.5% in constant currency on billable hours down 31.5%, in its fiscal Q3 ended 28 February 2026. That is a firm-level decline of exactly the magnitude the question needs, which is worth noting because it shows the bar is physically reachable. But RGP is an interim-talent and project-staffing business at the commodity end, the release attributes performance to cost alignment, segment repositioning and demand, and management's stated priority is 'scaling our Consulting segment' with investment intended to drive growth back. No AI attribution. Plus 0.3pp on demonstrated magnitude, no weight on attribution. And proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 on machine-generated evidence: approved by the Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure on 10 June 2025, comment period closed 16 February 2026, earliest effective date 1 December 2027. It legitimises a pathway for AI output offered without a human expert, but only through a Rule 702-style reliability gate, and it does not exist as law for the first third of my remaining window. Roughly plus 0.1pp net.

Hygiene, and it is the same failure mode for the third day running. The McKinsey 3,000-4,000 role claim resurfaced today on outsourceaccelerator, metaintro, finalroundai, programs.com and displaceindex, still with no FT, WSJ, Bloomberg or Reuters version, still traceable to the roughly 200 technology and support staff cut in November 2025. Not logged. A search result presented Faten Sabry's arrival at Compass Lexecon as August 2026 news; the press release is 21 April 2025. Andrew Swan's Cornerstone London hire was presented as 2026; it was effective 4 September 2024. And an aggregator claim that 54% of 2026 layoff events cite AI, affecting 170,945 workers, conflicts directly with Challenger's own 112,713 AI-cited cuts year to date, about 24% of the total. I am using Challenger.

Netting: roughly plus 1.1pp of up-weight against plus minus 1.4pp of down-weight, so about minus 1.0pp. That takes me from 11 to 10. I am trimming the top of the band from 19 to 18 because the forward guidance now on record from CRA, FTI and Huron all points the same way for the second half of 2026, which shortens the runway for the kind of inflection the upper tail requires. I am leaving the floor at 6.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is unchanged and remains a poor fit, which is still the dominant fact in this forecast. The class is: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with that loss attributed primarily to one identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Membership is sparse and every candidate fails at least one of the three conjoined criteria.

US travel agency employment fell roughly 40-50%, clearing the magnitude bar, but over roughly fifteen years from 1998 and with two distinct causes, online booking platforms and the abolition of airline commissions in 1995-2002. A resolver applying a primarily-attributed-to-one-technology test would very likely reject it. Contract document review contracted sharply once predictive coding and technology-assisted review became defensible in US discovery, but the affected population was contract attorneys and staffing agencies rather than a profession, and legal services revenue grew throughout; the Birjandi and Zadeh piece makes the same distinction when it says price sensitivity in expert testimony does not apply 'to, say, document review'. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third with desktop publishing as a clean single cause, but over more than a decade and against a physical craft with no advisory, judgement or relationship component. Bank tellers declined slowly and partially, with ATM deployment coinciding with two decades of branch expansion. Stock-photography contributors and switchboard operators are mismatched on either timescale or the professional-judgement dimension. Across the broader pool of technology-disruption episodes visible enough to be forecastable in advance, the modal outcome over five to six years is task recomposition with flat-to-rising sector employment, not a one-third contraction. Base rates for a named professional sector losing a third of value inside six years, technology-caused or otherwise, sit in the low single digits per episode.

The outside view therefore anchors at roughly 5-8% for the magnitude leg alone on a generic professional-services sector over 2024-2030. Two adjustments pull in opposite directions.

Upward: the inside view has real content, and today's addition sharpens it. The task profile of economic and management consulting maps unusually well onto current frontier-model capability in a way travel booking never mapped onto anything in 1995. Birjandi and Zadeh, writing in the Stigler Center's ProMarket, put the automatable share of the analytical layer at 45-70% depending on practice area and estimate 85-95% time savings on the maker-checker replication audit, 70-85% on data collection and 50-70% on quantitative modelling, and they name the equilibrium as a smaller industry by headcount with a hollowed-out middle tier of five-to-ten-year economists. Adoption is fast: Thomson Reuters has organisational genAI use in professional services at 40%, up from 22% a year earlier, and the MCA finds 77% of UK consulting firms have integrated AI or enabled employee use, with 76% deploying it for research tasks. The leverage pyramid that makes consulting profitable is exactly the layer under pressure, and the Big Four graduate intake data, KPMG down 29% from 1,399 to 942, Deloitte about 18%, EY 11%, PwC UK 6%, PwC US planning a 32% campus cut by 2028, shows firms acting on that belief with their own money. Agentic tooling that owns whole workflows rather than assisting single tasks is the specific capability shape that would make client-side insourcing cheap, and there is now a named live example of the demand side of that, with JPMorgan replacing external advisory functions with internal tools and the ACC's 2025 CLO survey finding a majority of large in-house departments deploying AI for previously outsourced work. RGP's fiscal Q3 2026 Consulting segment, minus 32.5% year on year on billable hours down 31.5%, at least demonstrates that a decline of the required magnitude is physically attainable inside twelve months at firm level. Four years and four months of runway remain. That argues for lifting the magnitude leg to perhaps 12-17% under a narrow reading isolating the expert-witness and competition-economics niche, and 4-6% under the broad BLS management, scientific and technical consulting aggregate.

Downward: the observed data run hard against the magnitude leg, and today's additions strengthen that side further. BLS series CES6054160001 stood at 1,886,600 in July 2026, with June's 1,888,100 the highest reading in the series' 36-year history, against a 2024 average of 1,860,500. The maximum drawdown in the entire series is 6.0%, in the February-April 2020 shock, recovered within a year. The question needs roughly minus 9.0% a year sustained for 53 consecutive months, and nothing in the series history is within a factor of five of that. The BLS itself, in the Monthly Labor Review 2024-34 projections, forecasts 9.4% employment growth for management, scientific and technical consulting services and ranks professional, scientific and technical services the second-fastest-growing sector overall at 7.5% growth and 812,500 net new jobs, naming AI-implementation demand as a driver rather than a threat. That sits alongside IBISWorld's July 2026 scientific and economic consulting figure of $65.6bn, up 2.6% on a 4.1% five-year CAGR with 16.4% margins, Mordor's 4.70% CAGR to $471.39bn by 2031, and the MCA's 5.7% and 7.4% UK growth projections for 2026 and 2027 with AI services the largest single driver. LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 places AI consultants and strategists second among fastest-growing US roles.

Within the narrow niche the comparators are dispersed but the forward guidance is uniformly upward. CRA reported $210.8m and plus 12.8% with consultant headcount up 3.3%, the first net increase in two years after a 5.8% fall in FY2024, and management now guides to mid-single-digit headcount growth by year-end 2026 with utilisation in the mid-to-upper 70s. FTI Economic Consulting reported $188.8m and minus 1.5% with headcount down 2.1% and margin at 4.7%, but posted a $13.2m sequential revenue improvement and management guided the segment to stop being a year-on-year drag from the second half of 2026. Huron has raised full-year 2026 guidance. BRG has opened Rome and Milan competition practices with economists poached from Brattle. The spread runs from minus 2% to plus 13% against a question asking about minus 33%; that is cyclical noise in a case-flow business, not the leading edge of a collapse.

Integrating: the magnitude leg sits at roughly 12-15% on a resolver-weighted blend of narrow and broad readings, and the attribution leg at roughly 0.65-0.72 conditional on a decline of that size occurring. Conditional on a genuine one-third collapse AI would almost certainly become the consensus explanation, but not certainly. FTI's disclosure remains the live worked example of the attribution problem, and RGP is now a second: the two consulting businesses in my file that are actually contracting attribute it to case flow and to demand and repositioning respectively, and neither names AI. The product lands at 8-11%. I sit at 10.
factors_up: The most on-point published analysis of this exact question now argues for a smaller industry (+3pp): Birjandi and Zadeh in ProMarket (Stigler Center, republished 25 August 2026, originally 29 April 2026, SSRN 7146120) put the AI-automatable share of the data, modelling and drafting layer at 50-60% in antitrust, 55-65% in securities fraud and commercial damages and 60-70% in employment discrimination, with 85-95% time savings on the maker-checker replication audit that structurally doubles senior billing. Their stated equilibrium is 'a smaller industry by headcount, more concentrated at the senior level, with a hollowed-out middle', with the five-to-ten-year economist tier compressing most sharply. They document the demand side too: JPMorgan replacing external advisory functions with internal AI, and the ACC 2025 Chief Legal Officer Survey finding a majority of large in-house departments deploying AI on previously outsourced work.

FTI Consulting 8-K of 30 July 2026 (+2pp): the Economic Consulting segment is the only one of five with falling billable headcount, 970 at 30 June 2026 against 991 a year earlier (-2.1%), while Corporate Finance rose 7.8% and Forensic and Litigation Consulting 3.0%; segment revenue -1.5% to $188.8m, utilisation down from 64% to 61%, adjusted segment EBITDA margin down from 7.4% to 4.7% (H1 0.8% versus 7.7%). This is the most literally on-point series available for the phrase 'economic consultancy'. I have cut this from 3pp to 2pp today because the same call disclosed a $13.2m sequential revenue improvement and management guidance that the segment stops being a year-on-year drag in H2.

Structural fee-model erosion (+3pp): roughly a quarter of McKinsey's global fees now outcome-based, BCG at about 25% of 2025 revenue from AI services (roughly $3.6bn) with AI and tech combined above 40%, Lilli running 500,000+ prompts a month with consultants citing up to 30% time savings. This is the clearest route to a value decline without a headcount collapse and the leg least visible in employment statistics. Hybridhero's 2026 analysis frames sustained client fee pressure and AI-changed delivery as jointly compressing margins even where revenue holds, and names the structural shift from time-billed to outcome-based and platform-subscription models.

Challenger July 2026 report of 6 August (+3pp): AI led all stated job-cut reasons for a fifth consecutive month at 10,970 cuts (33% of July's total), taking 2026 year-to-date AI-cited cuts to 112,713 (about 24% of all cuts) and cumulative since 2023 to 184,538. Bloomberg's 1 July 2026 analysis puts financial-activities and information payroll losses at an average 28,000 a month in 2026, accelerating, in the sectors with the fastest AI adoption. The August print due 4 September is the next scheduled test of whether the pattern spreads beyond Technology.

Graduate and entry-level pipeline still contracting on both sides of the Atlantic (+2pp): KPMG cut UK graduate and school-leaver intake 29% from 1,399 to 942, Deloitte about 18% from 1,700 to 1,400, EY 11% to 1,600, PwC UK 6% to 1,500; PwC US targets 2,197 campus associates by 2028 against 3,242 in FY2025, a 32% cut it links to 'the rapid pace of technological change'. KPMG's April 2026 cut of about 100 US audit partners alongside audit CTO Thomas Mackenzie's statement that within two to three years there will be 'next to no human beings' doing routine audit testing remains the sharpest insider testimony from an adjacent profession.

A decline of the required magnitude is demonstrably attainable at firm level, and equity markets have already repriced the sector (+2pp): Resources Connection reported fiscal Q3 2026 (quarter to 28 February 2026) Consulting segment revenue of $36.9m against $52.6m, -32.5% in constant currency on billable hours -31.5%. Gartner's Q2 2026 Consulting segment fell 8.8% year on year with gross contribution -12.6%. Financial-News puts Accenture down more than 57% of market value over twelve months and Capgemini nearly 40%, and Accenture's own new bookings fell 2% in the quarter to 31 May 2026. Equity value is not the resolution metric and RGP does not attribute its decline to AI, but the magnitude bar is not physically out of reach.
factors_down: BLS projects growth in exactly this industry over exactly this window (-5pp): the Monthly Labor Review 2024-34 industry and occupational projections forecast 9.4% employment growth for management, scientific and technical consulting services, explicitly naming demand for help implementing AI tools as a driver, and rank professional, scientific and technical services the second-fastest-growing sector overall at 7.5% growth and 812,500 net new jobs. That is roughly +0.9% a year from an official statistical agency with no commercial interest in the answer, against the -9.0% a year for 53 consecutive months the question requires, and it is immune to the commercial-interest objection available against IBISWorld and Mordor.

The narrow niche is guiding to growth, not contraction (-5pp): CRA's 6 August call reported record quarterly revenue of $210.8m (+12.8%), consultant headcount up 3.3% (the first net increase in two years after a 5.8% fall in FY2024), utilisation at 77%, eight practices growing and representing 95% of revenue, Antitrust and Competition Economics at a quarterly record, and management now guiding to mid-single-digit headcount growth by year-end 2026 with utilisation held in the mid-to-upper 70s. Paul Maleh: 'peak levels of new project opportunities and historically high conversion rates.' Huron raised FY2026 guidance to $1.85-1.89bn and $9.00-9.40 adjusted EPS on an AI-related pipeline. BRG has opened Rome and Milan competition practices with economists poached from Brattle; Cornerstone continues London and Brussels hiring.

The single most on-point analysis explicitly refuses to forecast an aggregate decline and argues pricing is sticky (-4pp): Birjandi and Zadeh conclude that 'industry employment will depend on whether AI-driven cost reductions generate enough new case volume to offset reduced labor demand per case. That demand-side question is an open question.' They argue AI cannot replace expert testimony and testifying-expert fees may rise; that high-stakes litigants shop on Daubert track record not price; that the pool of credible testifying experts is small enough to blunt fee competition; and that clients avoid opening an adversarial fee conversation with the expert they depend on in court. They identify new premium-fee lines with no methodological template: algorithmic price-fixing work following the DOJ's 2025 Statement of Interest, AI-system compliance and disparate-impact audits, and AI-amplified case screening.

Challenger July 2026 sector detail (-5pp): total US cuts 33,429, the lowest monthly total since July 2024 and down 46% year on year, with 477,033 cuts through July against 806,383 in the same period of 2025 (-41%) and hiring announcements up 25%; Services cuts, the consulting bucket, are 23,942 year to date, down 55% from 53,438; Technology accounts for 149,023 of 2026's cuts, up 67%. Andy Challenger states AI-related cutting 'has been limited outside of the Tech sector'. The concentration is not loosening.

The observed employment series is at an all-time high and the one contracting economic-consulting business names a non-AI cause (-4pp): CES6054160001 stood at 1,886,600 in July 2026 with June's 1,888,100 the highest in 36 years against a 2024 average of 1,860,500; maximum drawdown in series history is 6.0%. FTI attributes its Economic Consulting decline to lower demand for non-M&A antitrust and international arbitration work while litigating FTI v. Orszag et al. over expert defections to Econic Partners, and guided on 30 July that the segment will no longer be a year-on-year drag from H2 2026. RGP, the other contracting consulting segment in my file, names cost alignment, repositioning and demand, and its stated priority is 'scaling our Consulting segment'.

The attribution bar looks harder to clear, not easier, and the courtroom gate is being formalised (-3pp): a February 2026 survey of about 6,000 C-suite executives across four countries found 80%+ reporting no AI impact on productivity or employment; SHRM's 2026 survey finds client preference the most common non-technical barrier to displacement, present in 62.7% of jobs with any such barrier, which binds hardest in expert testimony where the client is a court. Proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 on machine-generated evidence, approved by the Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure on 10 June 2025 with comments closed 16 February 2026, would take effect no earlier than 1 December 2027 and imposes a Rule 702-style reliability showing, keeping a credentialed human in the loop for most of the remaining window. Sector revenue forecasts stay positive throughout: IBISWorld $65.6bn (+2.6%), Mordor 4.70% CAGR to $471.39bn by 2031, MCA 5.7% and 7.4% UK growth, LinkedIn ranking AI consultants and strategists the second fastest-growing US role.
key_uncertainties: Whether FTI's Economic Consulting contraction is the leading edge of something or pure idiosyncrasy. One quarter of -1.5% revenue and -2.1% headcount, with the firm blaming antitrust case flow while suing a breakaway competitor over expert defections, is what a cyclical trough plus a talent shock looks like; management has now guided to no year-on-year drag from H2, and CRA's +12.8% and +3.3% in the same quarter and niche argues idiosyncrasy. Late October gives a clean second reading on both.

How the resolver scopes 'economic consultancy'. The narrow expert-witness and competition-economics niche could diverge enormously by 2030 from the BLS management, scientific and technical consulting aggregate that the agency projects growing 9.4% to 2034, and the two readings imply magnitude-leg probabilities differing by a factor of three.

Whether the hollowed-out-middle thesis, which is now the mainstream expert view rather than a fringe one, converts into an aggregate revenue or headcount decline at all. Birjandi and Zadeh predict compression of the analyst and mid-tier economist layers alongside rising senior fees and new service lines; that is a compositional shift that could leave both revenue and total headcount roughly flat while transforming the profession completely.

Whether the attribution requirement is satisfiable in practice, given that any 2026-30 contraction will have overlapping macro, regulatory, offshoring and AI causes, that the two consulting businesses currently contracting in my file (FTI Economic Consulting and RGP Consulting) both name non-AI causes, and that Challenger expects tracking to become more opaque as regulation arrives.

Whether efficiency gains pass through to clients or are captured by firms. The legal analogue is discouraging for the question: law firm revenue rose 13% and net income 17% in 2024 while AI compressed task time, and BigHand found every firm surveyed said AI had affected pricing strategy but only a third had changed their pricing model. FTI's Economic Consulting average billable rate rose from $593 to $633 even as utilisation fell, which is the opposite of a price-collapse signature.

Whether client-side insourcing crosses a threshold. JPMorgan replacing external advisory functions and the ACC's finding that most large in-house departments now deploy AI on previously outsourced work are early but real; the binding constraint is court and regulator acceptance, and proposed FRE 707 will not take effect before 1 December 2027 and then imposes a Rule 702-style reliability gate. This remains the 2029-30 tail I cannot bound with any reference class.
update_triggers: Revise UP if FTI's Q3 2026 print (late October) shows Economic Consulting billable headcount falling a second consecutive quarter, or segment revenue declining more than 5% year on year against management's guidance that the segment stops being a drag in H2, or the promised 270-graduate Q3 intake failing to materialise

Revise UP if BLS series CES6054160001 falls for three consecutive months by a cumulative 2% or more, or if the 4 September 2026 print revises June-July 2026 below 1,860,000, or if BLS revises down its 2024-34 projection of 9.4% growth for NAICS 5416

Revise UP if the Challenger August report (due 4 September) shows AI-attributed cuts spreading materially outside Technology, specifically Services-sector AI-cited cuts exceeding 5,000 in any single month, reversing the current 55% year-on-year decline in Services cuts

Revise UP if CRA misses its stated guidance of mid-single-digit consultant headcount growth by year-end 2026, or if Huron, Cornerstone, NERA, Compass Lexecon, Brattle, Bates White or Analysis Group discloses a year-on-year consultant headcount fall of 10% or more or cuts guidance citing AI-driven client insourcing or fee compression

Revise UP if two or more of Source Global Research, IBISWorld, the Financial Times, the ONS, S&P Global or a peer-reviewed study publish quantified estimates of AI-caused consultancy revenue or headcount decline exceeding 15% from a 2024 base, or if Birjandi and Zadeh or comparable authors publish a follow-up that resolves their 'open question' toward net contraction with a number attached; or if a court admits AI-generated economic analysis in place of a testifying expert under proposed FRE 707

Revise DOWN if CRA's Q3 CY2026 print confirms continued consultant headcount growth toward its mid-single-digit target and a second consecutive record quarter in Antitrust and Competition Economics, or if FTI's Q3 print shows Economic Consulting back to year-on-year growth as management guided, or if the MCA's 2027 report confirms 7.4% UK growth alongside stable consultant headcount, or if the NY Fed, PIIE, the Hamilton Project, Indeed Hiring Lab or SHRM publish 2026-27 vintage work finding no measurable AI displacement effect in professional and business services

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 52 to 51. The six-day polling drought broke and for the first time in a week I have genuine fieldwork rather than a static average to reason from. Two polls landed with fieldwork ending 24 August. YouGov surveyed 23-24 August on n=2,380 and returned Reform 23 (-1 on its 16-17 August wave), Labour 22 (unchanged), Conservatives 20 (+1), Greens 13 (unchanged), Liberal Democrats 13 (+1), Restore Britain 3 (-1), SNP 3, Plaid 1, Your Party 0. Deltapoll, fieldwork ending 24 August on n=2,022, returned Labour 30, Reform 27, Conservatives 20, Lib Dems 8, Greens 8. Read within-pollster, both are mildly good for Labour. YouGov's Reform lead halves from two points to one; Deltapoll's Labour lead widens from two to three on Labour's highest share of the entire cycle from that house. YouGov's own writeup is appropriately deflationary: every party sits inside the margin of error of the previous wave, and Labour and Reform have both been penned between 22 and 24 in its tracker all month.

Read through the aggregates the picture is slightly the other way, and this is the tension I have to resolve rather than pick a side of. PollCheck's seven-poll moving average, stamped 25 August, now reads Labour 25.6, Reform 25.0, Conservatives 19.7, Greens 10.7, Lib Dems 10.4. That is a Labour lead of 0.6 against the 1.0 I recorded for three straight days. BritPolls' live ticker has gone further and now shows Reform 24.6 and Labour 24.6 - a dead tie, where yesterday it had Labour 25.4 to Reform 25.0. I do not think this is decay. It is composition: the seven-poll window has rolled off older, Labour-friendlier surveys and the incoming pair, while internally favourable, arrive at levels (Lab 22 from YouGov) below the average they are entering. The cleaner signal is the within-pollster movement, and that is pro-Labour. But I am not entitled to bank the within-pollster reading and ignore the aggregate when the aggregate is the object my seat models actually consume. I call the polling day a wash, tilted a hair negative.

The clearest thing I have to do today is retract yesterday's move. I raised the forecast a point in part on a supposed shift in the Ladbrokes timing book, from 2029-or-later at 10/11 to 1/1, which I read as the market shortening its expected horizon and therefore shrinking my decay discount. That was almost certainly an artefact of comparing two different sources at two different dates. The 10/11 figure comes from an OLBG page whose byline reads 'Updated: Feb 25' and whose copy still describes 'Sir Keir Starmer's party' - it is a February 2026 snapshot, not a current one. The Ladbrokes board itself, refetched today, prices 2029 or later at 1/1, 2028 at 7/2, 2027 at 9/4 and 2026 at 16/1, exactly as yesterday. I have no evidence the timing market moved at all. That +1pp comes straight back out. It is a useful reminder that on a question this thinly traded, the difference between a live price and a cached marketing page is the difference between signal and noise, and I got it wrong yesterday.

The most-seats board itself is unchanged and stable: Labour 11/8, Reform 11/5, Conservatives 7/2, Greens 33/1, Restore Britain 20/1, Liberal Democrats 40/1. Normalising that 105.7 per cent book gives Labour 39.8 per cent, Reform 31.3, Conservatives 22.2 - the same reading as yesterday and the day before. The majority book is likewise unchanged, with No Overall Majority at 4/7 and a Labour majority at 4/1. One genuine change: the 'Hung Parliament and Reform UK win most seats' special is 3/1 on today's Ladbrokes board, against 5/4 on the stale February page, which is a large drift against Reform over the intervening six months and is consistent with everything else.

Against that retraction I have two real additions. The first partially rescues the market-corroboration trigger I retired yesterday for want of a second venue. ElectaMeter, a composite UK political index last updated 23 August, explicitly lists Smarkets, Manifold Markets and UK bookmakers via BettingLounge among its sources alongside Electoral Calculus. It puts Labour's implied betting probability at 42.3 per cent against Reform's 33 per cent, and scores Labour 71 on its balanced index against Reform 60, blending a 25.5 per cent poll average, that 42.3 per cent market read and Electoral Calculus's 244 projected seats. So the liquid venues do get aggregated somewhere, and the multi-venue read sits about two and a half points above my Ladbrokes normalisation. That is worth a point.

The second is macroeconomic and I had not been carrying it at all. GfK's consumer confidence index rose to -14 in August, up three points, the fourth consecutive monthly rise, with the sub-index on personal finances over the next twelve months at +4 against -23 for the general economic outlook. Neil Bellamy of GfK attributed it to people having 'greater faith' in Healey and Burnham, while cautioning it is 'too soon to tell'. The British Retail Consortium recorded a parallel bump, with Helen Dickinson calling it a 'honeymoon boost driven by less pessimism about the outlook'. Sentiment turning up four months running is the single most plausible mechanism by which a Burnham bounce becomes something other than a bounce, and it is the first hard non-polling indicator I have seen pointing that way. Worth a point.

But the Budget risk has sharpened as well, and I am not going to net the good news without the bad. City AM's 25 August anatomy of the 28 October Budget puts Healey's shortfall at GBP 22bn after early spending pledges - close enough to the NIESR GBP 24bn I already carry - and notes gilt yields climbing to their highest level this century, with the Iran war having pushed up borrowing costs. Inflation is back to 2.9 per cent, a four-month high, which cuts directly against the cost-of-living framing. The tax menu on the table includes equalising capital gains with income tax (roughly GBP 14bn), extending national insurance to investment, property and pension income (roughly GBP 22bn, and described by Panmure Liberum's Simon French as the area most targeted, though 'deeply unpopular'), ending the pension tax-free lump sum, and a bank windfall levy. Burnham has already shut down the land value tax speculation. The manifesto lock on income tax, NI and VAT survives in letter, but an NICs base extension is exactly the sort of workaround that reads as a breach to voters. I also note the VAT removal from electricity bills is explicitly temporary, which is weaker than I framed it yesterday.

The last negative is Restore Britain, and it keeps going the wrong way for my biggest UP factor. YouGov has it at 3 per cent, down one on the fortnight, and PollCheck's tracker average is also 3.0. Electoral Calculus's June MRP assumed 7. Every seat model that gives Labour a plurality from vote-share parity is leaning on a three-way split of the right; if Restore Britain is really a three-point party rather than a seven-point one, that split is narrower than modelled and Labour's efficiency advantage is smaller. Netting it all: minus one for the retraction, plus one for the second-venue market read, plus one for consumer confidence, minus one for the aggregate slippage, minus a half for Restore Britain, and no change from Electoral Calculus, which is now thirty days stale at 28 July. One point down.
forecasts.base_rate:
The obvious reference class - incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election - gives roughly 65-70 per cent for the incumbent remaining largest party, about thirteen of nineteen defences since 1945. I continue to treat it as badly mis-specified and use it only as a loose upper anchor. Every case in that class comes from a two-and-a-half party system in which the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent. No governing party in that set ever entered mid-term polling at 22-30 per cent with four rivals at or above 8 per cent. Today's PollCheck seven-poll average has five parties between 10.4 and 25.6, and today's YouGov wave has five parties between 13 and 23. Sample of nineteen, poor fit, no more than a fifth of my weight.

A second class - governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then contested the following election - fits better and flatters less, though it splits sharply. Major, Brown, May, Johnson and Sunak: two of five were largest party at the next contest, a base rate near 40 per cent on a sample of five, and contaminated, because mid-term leader changes are usually a symptom of an already-losing position rather than a cure for one. Burnham differs measurably. The change has been followed by a genuine recovery: from 16-20 per cent in YouGov's series across Starmer's last six months to 22-24 since; from a six-point Reform lead in Electoral Calculus's June aggregate to a fractional Labour lead now; and to a personal rating YouGov calls the best for any prime minister on its ten-year tracker since Boris Johnson in May 2020. Post-Major and post-Brown produced no such recovery; post-Johnson under Sunak produced a partial one that decayed within months. So this class is informative about the risk of decay rather than about the starting level, and Richard Rose's 30 July judgement for Electoral Calculus that the Burnham advantage 'will fade rapidly' is the mainstream expert prior on exactly that decay.

What I have added to the outside view today is a non-polling leading indicator that speaks to the decay question directly. The standard post-honeymoon pattern is that leader ratings hold up for a while but economic sentiment never turns, so the vote share drifts back as the personal rating is gradually decoupled from the party's. Here economic sentiment is turning: GfK's index is at -14 in August, its fourth consecutive monthly rise, and the personal-finances sub-index is positive at +4. That does not tell me the bounce is permanent - inflation is back at 2.9 per cent and there is a consolidating Budget in nine weeks - but it does mean the mechanism that killed the Sunak recovery is not currently operating in the same direction. I do not have a clean historical base rate for 'incumbent recovery survives when consumer confidence is rising into a consolidating Budget', and I should be honest that I am reasoning by mechanism rather than by frequency here.

The third and most load-bearing consideration remains structural rather than historical: the seat-vote translation. Electoral Calculus's poll-of-polls, still dated 28 July on 13,321 respondents polled 7-27 July, returns Labour 244 seats on 23.9 per cent against Reform 127 on 23.4 - roughly ten Labour MPs per point of national vote against just over five for Reform - with the Conservatives on 132, Lib Dems 70, SNP 44 and Greens 10. Its 23-30 June MRP for PLMR (n=5,545) turned Labour 22 equals Reform 22 into Labour 217, Conservatives 151, Reform 127, Lib Dems 72, Greens 30, SNP 28. Convergent's 25-30 July MRP returns Labour 245 against Reform 174 and Conservatives 99 on Labour 26.1 to Reform 23.2. PollCheck's own constituency-level demographic projection tells a similar story. In every one of these Labour is largest from vote-share parity or a low single-digit lead, because Labour's shallow 33.7 per cent 2024 coalition remains geographically efficient while the right-of-centre vote splits three ways between Reform, the Conservatives and Restore Britain. Electoral Calculus's tactical-voting adjustment adds a further Reform penalty.

I continue to discount that mechanism from where I had it a fortnight ago, and today's YouGov reading pushes me further. The magnitude depends on how large Restore Britain really is, and direct measurement keeps disagreeing with the modelling assumption. YouGov now has Restore Britain at 3 per cent, down a point; PollCheck's dedicated tracker average is also 3.0, from Survation 2.0, YouGov 4.0 and Ipsos 4.0; Electoral Calculus's June MRP attributed 7. Only three of eleven active pollsters prompt for the party by name, so unprompted Restore Britain support may be sitting inside Reform's numbers rather than outside them - which would make the right less split, not more. Pulling the other way is the only hard electoral test: Makerfield on 18 June 2026, where Rebecca Shepherd took 6.8 per cent (3,111 votes), third of six and ahead of the Conservatives on 2.2 per cent, in a seat where Reform were 2024 runners-up. A real ballot beats a prompt-list artefact, but one ballot is one ballot, and the prompted series is trending down. Integration. I take the structural seat evidence as implying roughly 55-58 per cent for Labour largest on an election-now basis, which is where Electoral Calculus itself sits at 58 per cent. I discount five to eight points for the horizon. The Ladbrokes timing book prices 2029-or-later at 1/1 and, once the 108.9 per cent book is normalised, puts a little under half the mass on a contest before 2029, so the modal election is still two to three years away and three years of decay in a shallow 26 per cent coalition remains the dominant risk. Normalising the Ladbrokes most-seats book of 105.7 per cent gives Labour 39.8 per cent, Reform 31.3, Conservatives 22.2; ElectaMeter's multi-venue aggregate, which includes Smarkets and Manifold, reads Labour 42.3 per cent. I now have two market reads within two and a half points of each other, which raises my confidence in the market number without changing it much. That lands in the low fifties. I stay just above 50 because the seat arithmetic is a real, quantified and repeatedly replicated asymmetry rather than a tie. The 35-63 interval reflects Electoral Calculus's own 90 per cent seat ranges of 88-357 for Labour and 53-289 for Reform: the structural uncertainty over this horizon is enormous, and the gap between a 58 per cent model and a 40-42 per cent market is an honest statement of how little anyone knows.

Reform's organisational decay is now quantified and its leader's legal exposure is broadening. Restore Britain keeps shrinking on direct measurement, which undercuts the three-way right split that drives Labour's seat advantage in every MRP. Richard Rose's judgement for Electoral Calculus on 30 July that the Burnham advantage 'will fade rapidly' once he owns the cost of living, and that unpopular cuts or tax rises would see Labour 'dribble down to 20pc or lower', remains the mainstream expert prior and remains unfalsified. Labour's seat advantage in every MRP depends materially on which is right, and eight of eleven active pollsters do not prompt for the party at all.

Whether today's within-pollster improvement or today's aggregate slippage is the better signal. YouGov cut Reform's lead to one and Deltapoll widened Labour's to three, yet PollCheck's seven-poll average fell from a 1.0 to a 0.6 Labour lead and BritPolls flipped to a dead tie. Whether the eighteen-point gap between Electoral Calculus's 58 per cent and the bookmakers' normalised 40 per cent reflects favourite-longshot bias, model over-confidence in the seat-vote curve, or a real informational edge held by traders. ElectaMeter's multi-venue 42.3 per cent narrows the gap slightly and gives me a second read for the first time, but my central still sits between the two largely by construction.

How the 28 October Budget lands against a GBP 22-24bn shortfall, gilt yields at century highs and inflation back at 2.9 per cent, under a chancellor two thirds of the public cannot rate. The specific question is whether an NICs base extension or CGT equalisation is treated by voters as honouring or breaking the 2024 manifesto lock, and whether the four-month run of rising consumer confidence survives contact with it.

Where the Farage jeopardy lands and whether any of it touches Reform's vote. Ladbrokes prices him at 5/2 to be replaced as leader during 2026 and only 8/13 to lead Reform into the next election - yet Reform's vote has proved repeatedly indifferent to his personal ratings.

Whether Reform can build candidate and organisational capacity to convert a mid-20s national share into seats. Best for Britain's tracker has it shedding a councillor every three days since May, 35 in total, and its own leaked training material names internal failure as the biggest threat - but Reform starts as favourite in both council by-elections being held on 27 August, in Southey and in Throckley, Walbottle and Newburn.
