forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 84 to 83. A genuine down-trigger fired today, but on a horizon that mutes most of it, so the move is one point rather than three.

The substantive new number is the Kalshi KXOAIAGI ladder, fetched live this morning. It now reads 6 per cent before 2027 (up 1), 18 per cent before 2028 (down 3) and 36 per cent before 2030 (down 7.2), on 894,366 dollars of volume. The standing quote for OpenAI AGI by 2030 through April and mid-July was roughly 55 per cent. So this is a decline of about 19 points over six weeks and 7.2 points in a single session, on the deepest AGI-declaration book on the platform, roughly ten times the volume of the any-company series. That is not thin-volume noise and I will not dismiss it as such.

But the discipline here is to notice what did not move. KXAGICO-COMP, whose rules text matches this question's first limb almost exactly and expressly excludes 'AGI-like' and 'near-AGI' hedges, is literally unchanged: 41 per cent before 1 January 2028, 42 per cent before 1 April 2028, 59 per cent before 1 July 2028, on 92,192 dollars of volume. Same three prices, same volume figure, as yesterday. The any-company announcement market, the one that actually matches my resolution criteria, sat still while the OpenAI-specific pre-2030 book repriced.

The driver is legible. OpenAI's largest planned frontier reinforcement-learning run remains on hold with no confirmed end date. The 18 August announcement on pacing model development for cyber capabilities is still the operative state as of the 25 August coverage: many narrower workloads have restarted, but significant Astra and cyber workloads are still frozen, expanded monitoring consumes roughly 20 per cent of the compute of the process being watched against a 30-minute human-alert target, the Hugging Face postmortem is unpublished, and the evidence behind Astra's possible Critical cyber rating is unpublished. Astra, worth noting, was not the model in the July Hugging Face breach; it is a separate unreleased system. Mia Glaese, who runs safety and alignment there, put it plainly: 'We are very far from everything running back to normal.' I had the breach and the subpoena logged; what I had not properly priced is the structural point that the 20 per cent monitoring tax is permanent and scales with capability, with the largest runs explicitly facing the highest bar before they resume.

Compounding it, WSJ reports OpenAI's head of data centres Chris Malone left last week, the fourth senior departure after CRO Denise Dresser, COO Brad Lightcap and Fidji Simo, and frames the exits as coming ahead of a 'planned 2027 listing'. My standing assumption was a September 2026 target with the public S-1 hitting EDGAR mid-to-late August. It is 26 August and no public prospectus has appeared. One of my clearest UP triggers, the S-1 framing a shipped system as AGI, has slipped roughly a year.

Why only one point, then. Because there is a difference between mass leaving the distribution and mass sliding right, and a 7.2-point fall in a before-2030 contract caused by a training pause with no end date is almost definitionally the latter. A pause is a delay mechanism. A 20 per cent monitoring overhead is a tax on effective compute, not a ceiling on it. Nine years absorbs both. This is exactly the asymmetry that separates this question from its 2030 sibling, and it is why the 2030 forecast should take the full weight of today's news and this one should not.

The up-side of the tape is unusually well aimed at my binding constraints. Skild AI released S1, a robotics foundation model that executes tasks up to ten minutes long from a single human video prompt with no fine-tuning, reporting 66 per cent success on unseen tasks against 9 per cent for language-prompted VLAs at the same 100,000-hour training scale, with demonstrations spanning pancake flipping, pour-over coffee, plant potting and kit assembly. Sequoia's Alfred Lin called single-prompt execution of long-horizon tasks 'a game changer'. This matters more than a generic robotics story because Metaculus 5121, my strictest anchor and the single largest brake on this forecast, carries a January 2033 median precisely because it demands broad robotic as well as cognitive capability. S1 attacks that specific reason. Caveats stand: self-reported, 66 per cent is not reliability, ten minutes is not a working day, and Lin is an investor talking his book.

Second, SemiAnalysis published its deep dive on OpenAI's Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip, taped out with Broadcom in 16 months on TSMC N3P. The B0 stepping hits 13.4 PFLOPs of MXFP4 at 700W against Rubin's 900-1,150W, pairs HBM4 at 15.4 TB/s, and posts over 700 tokens per second per user on DeepSeek R1 and about 1,400 on GPT-OSS; The Verge reports OpenAI's own benchmarks at 1.5 to 1.9 times more work per watt than Nvidia. Performance per watt is the correct metric against my minus-8-point compute ceiling, because what binds the 2030-2035 window is power and memory, not FLOPs. Roughly 2,300 GW sitting in US interconnection queues is indifferent to FLOPs and entirely sensitive to watts. Sixteen months from start to a competitive tape-out also says the custom-silicon escape route is faster than I had assumed; set alongside Anthropic's hire of TPU founder Amir Salek and Broadcom's 60-to-100bn dollar SPV, three of the four leading labs now have a credible path around Nvidia's 15-per-cent-plus 2027 price rise.

Third, and directly against a standing DOWN trigger, Dell'Oro raised its 2026 datacentre capex forecast above 1 trillion dollars, with the top five hyperscalers above 600bn in 2026, up 36 per cent on 2025 and roughly 75 per cent AI-directed. I was watching for a capex cut on power or memory constraints. The opposite happened. Also logged but not weighted: Anandkumar and Jenik launched Accelerated Understanding, an enterprise physics AI built on neural operators rather than Transformers, claiming ingestion of 5 trillion data points in a single prompt, about 5 million times what Anthropic and Google flagships handle. Architectural diversification is relevant to Hassabis's 'one or two more breakthroughs' framing, but Reuters is reporting a launch, not a result.

The sobering item cuts the other way and I want it on the record. BenchLM's ARC-AGI-3 leaderboard, updated 25 August, still has Claude Opus 5 at 30.2 per cent, GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.8 per cent and Claude Opus 4.8 at 1.5 per cent. The base-model board has not moved despite NVIDIA's AVO posting 100.00 on the public set. That is the cleanest available evidence that the harness cluster I have been treating as an up-signal, AVO plus Inherent's Faraday plus Apodex 1.1, is scaffolding built around static models rather than evidence that the underlying models improved. I hold the method-over-scale factor at plus 5 but I now read it as telling me about deployment rather than about the capability trend.

Other anchors are unchanged: Goodheart Labs aggregate median 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2043; Metaculus 5121 January 2033 and 3479 June 2028; LEAP wave 8's superforecaster median 2047 still unrefreshed. I should also log Samotsvety's January 2026 aggregate, eight forecasters, at roughly 28 per cent for AGI by 2030, which sits alongside LEAP on the sceptical side. Governance hardened non-specifically: Meta and 29 state attorneys general are in mid-trial settlement talks, Pennsylvania's AG sued Snap on 25 August, and AI Weekly has Regulation story volume up 1,400 per cent week on week. None of that is AGI-specific; all of it raises the cost of a lab's lawyers signing off on the word.

Netting: a deep real-money book moved against me by 7.2 points on a pre-2030 contract, the matching any-company book did not move at all, the frontier pause is a rightward shift rather than a truncation, and the day's structural news on robotics generalisation and performance per watt is aimed squarely at my two largest drags. Move to 83. I widen the lower bound one point to 72 because this is the first session in this run where a liquid market moved against the thesis by more than a rounding error, which argues my left tail was slightly too thin. Coherence check: 83 against Q1's 31 implies a 75.4 per cent conditional probability of a qualifying declaration during 2030-2035 given none by 2030, down from 76.8 per cent yesterday and comfortably above the 2030 number.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is no frequency base rate available here. AGI has never been developed, the event class has zero members, and no historical frequency exists. The only usable outside view is the distribution of published forecasts on near-identical questions, treated as a reference class of forecaster distributions rather than of events. I track seven anchors and weight them by how closely their resolution criteria match this question's, which is a rhetorical, announcement-shaped bar rather than a capability bar.

First, the cross-platform aggregate. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, which combines Metaculus 3479, Metaculus 5121, the Metaculus adversarial Turing question, Manifold's high-quality-Turing-test market and Kalshi, and is funded by Jaan Tallinn, reads a combined median of 2031 with an 80 per cent interval of 2027-2043. Fitting a right-skewed distribution through those percentiles puts roughly 69 to 75 per cent of mass before 1 January 2035. The asymmetry is load-bearing: four years separate the 10th from the 50th percentile but twelve separate the 50th from the 90th, so cumulative probability rises steeply through the late 2020s then flattens into a long tail that 2035 sits inside but not deep inside. This anchor has been static for three consecutive days.

Second, Metaculus's flagship strict question 5121. The community median for the first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced stands at January 2033, from a pool of more than 1,800 forecasters, with 25 per cent probability by 2029. That definition requires broad robotic as well as cognitive capability, the strictest common bar in the field, which mechanically pushes the median later than any announcement-based criterion. A January 2033 median implies roughly 60 to 68 per cent of mass before 2035, and this question's bar is materially easier. The weakly-general companion 3479 carries a June 2028 median. Direction matters: from 2025 into 2026 the Metaculus community pushed timelines out rather than in, which is the main reason I do not simply take the market-implied high-80s. Today's Skild S1 result is the first item in some weeks bearing directly on why 5121 sits latest, since a robotics foundation model executing ten-minute tasks from a single video prompt is progress on exactly the robotic limb of that definition.

Third, the announcement-shaped markets, which match this question's first limb most closely. Kalshi's KXAGICO-COMP series, 'Will any company achieve AGI before [date]?', resolves Yes only if a company explicitly states it has achieved, attained, reached or developed AGI; statements describing 'AGI-like', 'AGI-level', 'near-AGI' or 'toward AGI' systems expressly do not qualify. That rules text is close to this question's first limb. Fetched live today it reads 41 per cent before 1 January 2028, 42 per cent before 1 April 2028 and 59 per cent before 1 July 2028, on 92,192 dollars of volume, all three identical to yesterday, with previously logged tranches near 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031. On naive hazard continuation those extrapolate to the mid-to-high 80s by 2035. This is my most bullish anchor and also the one most exposed to the chip-and-memory saturation argument, since it assumes the post-2030 hazard rate matches the pre-2030 rate. Thin volume and wide spreads argue for treating the levels as indicative.

Fourth, and repriced today, the sceptical real-money end. Kalshi's OpenAI-specific KXOAIAGI ladder now reads 6 per cent before 2027, 18 per cent before 2028 and 36 per cent before 2030, on 894,366 dollars of volume, against a standing 55 per cent quote for by-2030 as recently as mid-July. Polymarket gives OpenAI about 9 per cent for AGI by 2027. Money is consistently more cautious than rhetoric, and this is now the deepest book in the category, so the 19-point six-week decline deserves real weight even though it is company-specific and pre-2030. The correct reading is that traders have pushed OpenAI's declaration mass to the right in response to the frontier training pause, the Astra Critical-cyber question, the Alabama subpoena and a listing that has slipped to 2027, rather than removing it from the distribution.

Fifth, the rigorously elicited expert panels, still the strongest brake. LEAP wave 8, fielded 20 April to 11 May 2026, puts the superforecaster median AGI year at 2047 with only 80 per cent before 2100, and economists at 60 per cent before 2100. Its more concrete elicitation is more bullish: for 80 per cent success on software tasks requiring eight hours or more of expert effort, the median expert gives 50 per cent by 2030 or earlier and the median superforecaster 2028. Wave 9 covered catastrophe and governance rather than timelines, so the 2047 median stands unrefreshed. Alongside it, Samotsvety's January 2026 aggregate, from eight forecasters, sits at roughly 28 per cent for AGI by 2030. If these are right, mass before 2035 is well under 40 per cent. I do not weight them heavily, because their definitions are stricter still and superforecaster panels have been systematically late on AI capability questions since 2021, but the spread between LEAP's 2047 and KXAGICO's implied high-80s by 2035 is wider than my entire confidence interval and is the honest reason the interval stays wide.

Sixth, the explicit structural models. The AI Futures Project's Q2.5 update of 16 August 2026 gives Automated Coder medians of November 2027 (Kokotajlo), January 2030 (Lifland) and January 2029 (Halstead), and TED-AI, their AGI analogue defined as at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks, at November 2028, July 2032 and April 2031 respectively. All three fall inside 2035. Halstead states the model's raw output is 'nearly 90%' on AC by January 2035 and hand-adjusts to 80 per cent. Critically, the authors now state that all their forecasts are conditional on things going as fast as is technically feasible, with no adjustment for government-imposed slowdown, and their own AI 2027 grading has reality running at 70 to 90 per cent of scenario pace. Treated unconditionally, these should be shaded down by whatever probability one assigns to a material non-technical brake over nine years, and OpenAI's own indefinite pause on its largest run is a live demonstration that such brakes are not hypothetical. Alongside them, FutureSearch's tracker records every updater between January and April 2026 moving earlier, and Christiano's March 2026 note puts us at the 90th percentile of his 2019 and 2021 timelines.

Seventh, lab-leader rhetoric, which sits earliest and which limb two of this question rewards: Altman placing AGI inside the current presidential term, Amodei's powerful AI by 2027, Hassabis at Davos in January 2026 at roughly 50 per cent by end of decade, Huang's March 2026 'we've achieved AGI' to Lex Fridman, Goertzel's AGI-26 remark, and Sequoia's '2026: This is AGI'. Hassabis moved from Google DeepMind CEO to chairman and Alphabet chief scientist on 5 August, which changes who speaks for the most definitionally careful of the big labs.

Weighting the strict-definition anchors at roughly 70 per cent and the announcement-shaped anchors at roughly 85 to 88, then adding for the second resolution limb, and subtracting for the possibility that no serious lab ever uses the word, which the 27 April 2026 removal of the OpenAI-Microsoft AGI clause made concrete, the outside view lands in the low-to-mid 80s. Today's repricing of the deepest declaration book pulls that to 83.

Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP, whose rules text matches this question's first limb almost exactly and expressly excludes 'AGI-like' and 'near-AGI' hedges, held completely firm through today's repricing elsewhere at 41 per cent before Jan 2028, 42 per cent before Apr 2028 and 59 per cent before Jul 2028 on 92,192 dollars of volume; the logged 70.5 per cent by 2030 and 76.5 per cent by 2031 tranches extrapolate to about 85-88 per cent by 2035. forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 7 to 8.

I have held at 7 for two weeks and I am moving up one point today, not because a threshold was crossed but because two pieces of evidence I had been treating as soft have hardened, and because I found an external anchor I had not previously priced that sits above my implied hazard rather than below it. This is a one-point move with a slightly fatter upper tail, not a regime change.

Start with the trigger checklist, which is mostly quiet. Taiwan's MND reported two PLA aircraft sorties, seven PLAN vessels and two official ships for 25 August, following two sorties, seven PLAN vessels and two official ships on the 24th, zero aircraft with seven PLAN and seven official ships on the 23rd, and three sorties with eight PLAN and seven official ships on the 22nd. The air component is pinned at its floor, the naval component is flat at seven to nine hulls, the coastguard component oscillates between two and seven. There is still no Fujian MSA navigation warning anywhere in August, still no named exercise since Justice Mission 2025 - eight full months, the longest gap since 2022 - and still no boarding of a Taiwan-bound merchant vessel under Coast Guard Order No. 3. None of the mobilisation indicators in trigger four have appeared. I will add one deflationary note on this week's readings: Typhoon Saudel is passing closest to Taiwan on Thursday and Friday, and the CWA has had torrential-rain warnings up across southern and eastern Taiwan since the 22nd. That is a mundane suppressor of flight operations, so I should not read this particular week's floor as signal in either direction.

The first hardening concerns US carrier posture. Yesterday I upgraded this factor on The War Zone's 17 August survey. Today's 24 August survey is more definite and worse. USS George Washington - the only forward-deployed carrier, homeported in Yokosuka - has transited the Malacca Strait and relieved USS Abraham Lincoln in the Arabian Sea; Lincoln is now transiting eastward across the Indian Ocean. TWZ's own summary of the 17 August edition put it bluntly: George Washington en route to relieve Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East, 'which leaves no carriers in the Pacific.' Theodore Roosevelt was still pierside in San Diego on 24 August. Carl Vinson departed San Diego on 10 August but is in Tailored Ship's Training Availability and Final Evaluation Period - basic workups, months from a deployment. So the position on 26 August is not a gap that closes in September; it is zero US carrier presence in the Pacific with the theatre's own permanently assigned carrier committed to CENTCOM. My third update trigger specified Theodore Roosevelt going to CENTCOM with no replacement assigned. Strictly that has not happened, but the functionally equivalent thing - the forward-deployed carrier leaving PACOM for CENTCOM with no replacement - has. I count that as a partial fire.

I should be honest about the counterweight, because it cuts against the confidence I expressed yesterday. TWZ's 11 August edition says Roosevelt's destination - CENTCOM to sustain dual-carrier coverage, or a western Pacific patrol - 'will likely depend on how the negotiations with Iran shake out.' That is a genuinely open question, not the settled CENTCOM assignment the 17 August framing implied. So the direction of the carrier factor is confirmed but its durability is less certain than I said. Those roughly cancel, and on their own would not have moved me.

What moved me is the market evidence. I had been anchoring on Polymarket's invasion markets: 4 percent for an invasion by 31 December 2026 on about forty million dollars of volume, 1 percent by 30 September. Today I looked at two markets I had not been tracking. The first is 'Will China blockade Taiwan in 2026?', trading at 6 percent on 261,491 dollars as of 25 August, and its resolution language is strikingly close to mine: it requires prevention of normal ingress or egress of foreign commercial traffic to Taiwan's main ports or airports by threat or use of force for at least 24 hours, declared or de facto, covering part or whole of the main island, established by broad consensus of credible reporting. It explicitly excludes drills with NOTAMs that do not materially deny access, excludes purely economic or coercive measures without physical interdiction, excludes islet-only incidents, and excludes seizure of a single vessel unless part of an enforced pattern. That is very nearly the question I am forecasting, with a 24-hour rather than 72-hour bar. Six percent for the remaining four months of 2026 is far above my implied near-term hazard, which is roughly one percent for the same period.

I do not take that at face value. The market is thin - 261,000 dollars and 28 comments - and the No side is paying 94 cents for a six-cent return over four months, roughly a 19 percent annualised yield, which is well above risk-free. That spread is the classic signature of long-shot bias and scarce No-side capital rather than genuine crowd belief. Annualising 6 percent over four months would imply something like 18 percent a year and 45 percent over my full window, which I regard as absurd. So I discount it heavily. But I cannot discount it to zero, and it is the closest-matched external estimate I have found for this question.

The second and better-capitalised anchor is 'Will China invade Taiwan by December 31, 2027?', at 12 percent on 3.03 million dollars as of 26 August. Its bar is looser than mine - any military offensive intended to establish control over any portion of ROC-administered inhabited territory, which would include Kinmen, Matsu or Pratas - but the arithmetic is instructive. Take 12 percent through end-2027 on the loose bar, apply the 25-to-35-percent narrowing factor I use for the strict blockade-or-assault-on-Taiwan-proper bar with two-agency confirmation, and you get roughly 4 percent through end-2027 on my terms. Add the 2028-29 period, where I think hazard is materially higher - PLA centenary milestone passed, command layer rebuilt, January 2028 Taiwan presidential election, the projected trough in US hull and munitions availability - and the implied total lands nearer 8 or 9 than 7. The deep market, properly translated, is not below me. It is slightly above me. Notably the invade-2026 market at 4 percent and the invade-2027 market at 12 percent are roughly consistent with a flat hazard, i.e. the crowd applies no term-structure discount at all.

One more item runs upward, and it firmed rather than softened today. The Taipei Times of 26 August reports that Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu opened interparty negotiations on 24 August over the DPP's NT$210 billion special budget act for coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones and uncrewed one-way strike boats. The KMT's counter-proposal offers a larger headline number, NT$240 billion, but disbursed at NT$40 billion a year over six years from the annual budget with the Ministry of Economic Affairs as lead agency; the TPP version specifies no funding source at all and explicitly refuses to fund uncrewed ground and surface vehicles. MND Comptroller Bureau head Hsieh Chi-hsien said last Thursday that the opposition bills would not fund the three uncrewed systems the armed forces planned to buy, and the 14 August passage of NT$19.2 billion covered unarmed drones and industry subsidies, not weapon systems. Because this year's and next year's annual budgets are already proposed, and Article 79 of the Budget Act reserves supplementary budgets to the Executive Yuan, the practical effect of the opposition route is that no money reaches the 210,000-drone programme until 2028 - a 17-month delay. That programme is the lynchpin of the hellscape concept, and the delay lands squarely in the years where most of this question's probability mass sits.

Against all of that, one clean piece of downward news. Xi's state visit is now dated and dual-confirmed: arriving Washington late on 23 September, White House talks with Trump on 24 September, departing on the 25th - his first US state visit in eleven years. Polymarket prices it 94 percent by 30 September and 97 percent by 31 December on 738,000 dollars. Yesterday I had only 'expected September'. A confirmed date is worth more than an expectation, and it reinforces the crowded near-term political calendar alongside the October fifth plenum and November APEC in Shenzhen.

Net: the carrier factor confirmed but with its durability more open, the drone-procurement delay firmed, a well-matched but thin market anchor and a deep market anchor both sitting above my number, against a firmer near-term diplomatic floor. Move to 8, interval 4 to 13.
forecasts.base_rate:
Four reference classes bear on this question, and I weight the first and fourth most heavily.

The broad class is major-power initiation of an opposed amphibious assault, or a sustained naval blockade of a defended and populated territory, since 1945. The candidate set is thin: Inchon in 1950 against a state already at war, Suez in 1956, the Cuban quarantine of 1962 which was a partial interdiction lasting under a month, the Falklands in 1982 which was a British counter-invasion of a lightly garrisoned archipelago, the Iran-Iraq tanker war of 1984-88, Russia's Black Sea grain interdiction from 2022, and the US naval blockade of Iran begun on 13 April 2026 and still running past four months. Roughly seven episodes across eighty years, against a denominator of perhaps twenty to thirty dyads at any time possessing both capability and a claimed casus belli. That implies an annualised hazard per capable dyad of roughly 0.5 to 2 percent. Applied to the 3.35 years from today to 1 January 2030, that yields about 2 to 7 percent. The Iran case is a live addition to the class, marginally raises its frequency, and demonstrates that the international system currently tolerates a great-power blockade of a state's seaborne trade without the initiator paying a prohibitive price - which argues for the upper end of that band.

The second class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes specifically. Since 1995 there have been seven salient ones: the 1995-96 missile crisis, the August 2022 post-Pelosi encirclement, Joint Sword 2024A in May and 2024B in October, Strait Thunder in April 2025, Justice Mission 2025 in December, and the January 2026 militia floating wall. None produced a blockade exceeding 72 hours or an assault. The longest disruption on record is roughly 30 hours in January 2026, when an L-shaped array of thousands of Fujian and Zhejiang fishing vessels spanning some 300 miles disrupted Strait traffic; the August 2022 closure areas were announced, time-boxed and did not produce interdiction that news agencies characterised as a blockade. A naive Laplace estimate on zero-for-seven gives roughly 11 percent per episode, and at the observed rate of about one episode every eighteen months one would expect two more before 2030, implying something above 20 percent. I reject that arithmetic. It treats deliberately calibrated signalling exercises as independent draws on a war lottery, when in every case the PRC controlled the end date in advance and announced it. The correct inference from this class is about the ceiling of routine coercion, not the hazard of a decision for war. The episode rate has itself fallen: PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan totalled 1,334 in H1 2026, more than halved year on year and the lowest since 2023 against more than 5,400 in all of 2025, with a record number of zero-detection days and no large-scale drill around the island in H1, the first such half-year since 2022.

The third class is deliberate irredentist initiation by a leader with a stated claim, capability and a domestic timeline: Argentina over the Falklands in 1982, Iraq over Kuwait in 1990, India over Goa in 1961, China over the Indian border in 1962, Russia over Crimea in 2014 and Ukraine in 2022. The class is not empty, strategic warning was short in most cases, and in several the initiator surprised analysts who had reasoned from cost. The common thread is that every initiator believed the operation would be short and cheap. That is the sharpest disanalogy here: the PLA's own literature treats a Taiwan landing as the hardest operation in modern warfare, and the quarantine option exists precisely because the assault option is not believed to be cheap. This class raises the floor and widens the upper tail; it does not set the central estimate.

The fourth consideration is the resolution bar and the shape of the hazard over the window. Decompose. The probability that Beijing initiates some materially escalated coercive action against Taiwan before 2030 - a declared quarantine, a customs-inspection regime, a closure area, an offshore-island seizure, a boarding of a Taiwan-bound merchant vessel - I put at 20 to 30 percent, and the accreting legal and militia infrastructure supports the upper half of that: the 2021 Coast Guard Law authorising force against foreign vessels in claimed waters, the 2021 revised Maritime Traffic Safety Law extending reporting obligations, Coast Guard Order No. 3 in force since 15 June 2024 permitting boarding, inspection and detention, Fuzhou's civilian vessel requisition regulations, and mandatory BeiDou and AIS fitment across Fujian's 12,000-plus registered fishing boats. But the conditional probability that such an action meets this question's terms - a blockade lasting more than 72 hours or an assault on Taiwan proper, confirmed by two or more major news agencies - is considerably lower, perhaps 25 to 35 percent. Beijing's revealed preference is for actions that are undeclared, sub-threshold, law-enforcement-framed and reversible, precisely because that forecloses third-party intervention. The product of those two ranges lands at roughly 5 to 10 percent.

Hazard is not uniform across the window. It is depressed through late 2026 by Xi's now-confirmed 23-25 September state visit to Washington, the fifth plenum called for October on party discipline rather than the five-year plan, November APEC in Shenzhen, 21st Party Congress preparation for 2027, and a CMC reduced to Xi plus Zhang Shengmin after the January 2026 removals of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. It rises through 2027-2029 with the PLA centenary capability milestone, the January 2028 Taiwan presidential election, a rebuilt command layer, the projected trough in US munitions and hull availability, the frozen 14 billion dollar arms package, the probable slip of Taiwan's 210,000-drone programme to 2028, and the prospect of extended periods with no US carrier in the western Pacific. Roughly 15 percent of the window's probability mass sits in the remainder of 2026, with the balance concentrated in 2028-29.

On external anchors, my read shifted today. The near-dated markets remain reassuring: Polymarket prices 96 percent no invasion by 31 December 2026 on about forty million dollars, and 99 percent by 30 September. But the longer-dated and better-matched markets sit above my number rather than below it. 'Will China invade Taiwan by December 31, 2027?' trades at 12 percent on 3.03 million dollars, on a looser bar than mine; translated through my 25-35 percent narrowing factor and extended over 2028-29, that implies 8 to 9 percent on my terms. And 'Will China blockade Taiwan in 2026?', whose resolution language closely tracks mine at a 24-hour rather than 72-hour threshold, trades at 6 percent on 261,000 dollars for the remaining four months of the year - a figure I discount heavily for thinness and long-shot bias but cannot ignore. The main limitation of all of these is definitional: none uses my exact bar, and the gap between a law-enforcement-framed quarantine and something two major agencies would call a blockade is where most of the disagreement lives. Blending: the outside-view class centres near 4 percent, the deliberate-decision class argues for a fatter tail, the decomposition centres near 7, and the market translation argues for 8 to 9. I take 8 percent with an interval of 4 to 13.
factors_up: Zero US carrier presence in the Pacific is now confirmed rather than projected (+2.5pp). The War Zone's 24 August survey has USS George Washington - the Yokosuka forward-deployed carrier - having transited the Malacca Strait and relieved USS Abraham Lincoln in the Arabian Sea, with Lincoln transiting eastward across the Indian Ocean; TWZ's 17 August edition put it as leaving 'no carriers in the Pacific'. Theodore Roosevelt was still pierside in San Diego on 24 August and Carl Vinson is in TSTA and FEP workups, months from deployable. Hudson's Bryan Clark's arithmetic - 11 carriers, two continuous deployments, two held for Iran, therefore months each year at zero Pacific presence - is now descriptive.

Taiwan's 210,000-drone asymmetric programme is on course to slip to 2028 (+2pp). Taipei Times, 26 August: Han Kuo-yu opened interparty negotiations on 24 August over the DPP's NT$210bn special budget act for coastal surveillance drones, coastal attack drones and one-way strike boats. The KMT counter disburses NT$240bn at NT$40bn a year over six years from the annual budget with MOEA in the lead; the TPP version names no funding source and refuses to fund uncrewed ground and surface vehicles. MND's Hsieh Chi-hsien says the opposition bills would not fund the three systems the armed forces planned to buy; with annual budgets already proposed and Article 79 reserving supplementary budgets to the Executive Yuan, the practical effect is no money until 2028 - a 17-month delay in the lynchpin of the hellscape concept.

The best-matched external market anchors sit above my estimate, not below it (+1.5pp). Polymarket's 'Will China blockade Taiwan in 2026?' trades at 6 percent on $261,491 as of 25 August, on resolution language closely tracking mine at a 24-hour rather than 72-hour bar. 'Will China invade Taiwan by December 31, 2027?' trades at 12 percent on $3.03m as of 26 August on a looser bar; translated through my narrowing factor and extended across 2028-29, that implies 8-9 percent on my terms. The deep market applies no term-structure discount between its 2026 and 2027 contracts.

The 14 billion dollar Taiwan arms package remains frozen (+1.5pp). The Washington Post reported on 23 May 2026 that the January package was paused after the Beijing summit; acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said it was held to secure munitions for Epic Fury. FAPA's 8 June bulletin still describes it as under review, Lai was publicly asking for approval on 18 June, and I can find no evidence of release. Three months of freeze on top of the existing delivery backlog subtracts from Taiwan's 2027-29 capability curve.

Quarantine infrastructure and its legal-normative groundwork continue to accrete (+1.5pp). The 2021 Coast Guard Law, the 2021 revised Maritime Traffic Safety Law and Coast Guard Order No. 3 in force since 15 June 2024 together authorise boarding, inspection and detention in claimed waters. Since 1 June 2026 Yushan-class cutters have patrolled east of Taiwan; between 6 and 10 June Haixun 09 and Haixun 06 covered 1,030 nautical miles and radio-verified 198 passing ships. On 11-12 August the PLAN ran a first-ever joint navigation exercise with Indonesia's KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai east of Taiwan, framed by Global Times as demonstrating PRC jurisdiction over the EEZ east of Taiwan island.

The US-Iran war is normalising sustained maritime interdiction, and salami-slicing continues elsewhere (+1pp). CENTCOM's blockade, imposed 13 April 2026, had redirected 70 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 by 24 August. Separately, Reuters reported on 19 August, from 19 July Vantor satellite imagery, that China has completed the first phase of reclamation at Antelope Reef in the Paracels - a feature Taiwan also claims - with a helicopter pad under construction in what analysts call its largest military base. AMTI records 933 CCG ship-days at Scarborough in H1 2026, nearly matching all of 2025.
factors_down: Xi's state visit to Washington is now dated and dual-confirmed (-2pp). Arriving late on 23 September, White House talks with Trump on 24 September, departing 25 September - his first US state visit in eleven years, with trade, AI governance, Taiwan and the Strait of Hormuz on the agenda. Polymarket prices it 94 percent by 30 September and 97 percent by 31 December on $738,392. A confirmed date is stronger evidence than an expectation, and it sits alongside the October fifth plenum on strict party governance and November APEC in Shenzhen in a crowded near-term political calendar.

Two independent expert teams have examined a 2026 PLA lull for pre-campaign signatures and found none (-2.5pp). The Taiwan Security Monitor's four-author Schar School study of 7 March 2026 worked through five hypotheses for the 27 February to 5 March stand-down and rejected incapacity, fuel conservation and invasion preparation, concluding it was routine variability; Drew Thompson reached the same conclusion on 6 March by a different route. Their invasion-prep argument - that a theatre-level operation generates detectable naval redeployment, airbase and logistics signatures - remains the single strongest structural check, and none of those signatures has appeared six months on.

PLA air tempo is structurally halved and has stayed there (-2pp). SCMP's tally of MND data on 24 July 2026 gives 1,334 PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan in H1 2026, more than halved year on year and the lowest since 2023 against more than 5,400 in all of 2025, with a record number of zero-detection days and no large-scale drill around the island in H1. The 22-25 August readings of 3, 0, 2 and 2 sorties sit on that trend line, though Typhoon Saudel and a week of torrential-rain warnings mean this particular week's numbers carry less information than usual.

Zero-for-seven record of salient Strait coercion episodes since 1995 converting into a sustained blockade or assault, against a strict resolution bar (-2pp). The longest disruption on record is about 30 hours, in January 2026. GTI's 12 August analysis argues Beijing prefers a declared quarantine precisely because it is law-enforcement-framed and reversible, whereas a blockade is a state-versus-state act likely to draw US, Japanese or Philippine intervention - so the instrument being built is the one least likely to be reported by two agencies as a blockade. Polymarket still prices 96 percent no invasion by end-2026 on about $40m, down from near 30 percent YES in late 2025.

No operational signalling and a still-gutted command layer (-1.5pp). No Fujian MSA navigation warning, NOTAM or closure area anywhere in August 2026, the most recent being Zhangzhou MSA on 22 July for drills within 12km of the Dongshan coast; eight months with no named exercise since Justice Mission 2025, the longest gap since 2022; no reservist call-up, RO-RO requisition, ammunition prepositioning or medical surge. Over 100 officers removed since 2022 with the CMC reduced to Xi plus Zhang Shengmin and no reconstitution reported through the 21 August ISW-AEI update.

Beijing keeps declining clean opportunities to escalate, and Roosevelt's destination is not settled (-1.5pp). It waited until the final day of Han Kuang 41 - which included a first-ever Navy and Coast Guard counter-blockade drill - to have spokesperson Chen Xi dismiss it on 14 August as a posturing, wasteful charade, with no counter-exercise, and answered Lai's hawkish 23 August Kinmen speech on the 68th anniversary of the 823 bombardment with two aircraft and two official ships. It tracked the 21 August US P-8A Strait transit and said the situation was under control. Separately, TWZ's 11 August survey says Theodore Roosevelt's September assignment - CENTCOM or a western Pacific patrol - depends on how the Iran negotiations resolve, so the Pacific gap is not yet locked in for 2027-29.
key_uncertainties: Why PLA air activity has been structurally halved all year. Deliberate de-escalation with substitution toward coastguard coercion, disruption from the purge of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli, and pre-campaign resource conservation imply very different hazard rates. Two independent teams rejected the third for the February episode and the corroborating indications and warnings are still absent, but the seven-month persistence of the drop is not explained by the seasonality they invoke

Whether Theodore Roosevelt fills the western Pacific or goes to CENTCOM, and how long the Pacific carrier vacancy lasts. TWZ's 11 August read makes it contingent on the Iran negotiations; the 17 and 24 August reads suggest CENTCOM. If two carriers stay committed to Iran through 2027-29 this is a structural change in the deterrence environment rather than a weeks-long blip, and the single most likely route to my having to revise materially up

How to weight thin, long-shot-biased prediction markets whose resolution language matches mine closely against deep markets whose language does not. The 6 percent blockade-2026 contract on $261k and the 12 percent invade-2027 contract on $3.03m point the same direction - above my number - but for different and partly non-credible reasons, and I may be over-correcting toward crowd noise

Whether the 14 billion dollar arms package is released, and how much of Taiwan's 2027-29 capability curve the pause plus the pre-existing backlog plus a probable 17-month drone-programme delay has already removed. Munitions competition with the Iran campaign is a durable constraint that does not resolve when the package is unfrozen

Whether a sub-72-hour or law-enforcement-framed quarantine, which the January 2026 floating wall, Coast Guard Order No. 3, the eastern patrols since 1 June and Taiwan's own 25 June tabletop all suggest is the modal escalation, would be described by two major agencies as a blockade. This is a resolution-language risk as much as a real-world one, now complicated by 'blockade' having acquired a vivid contemporary referent in the US operation against Iran

How the 28 November 2026 local elections and the January 2028 presidential election are read in Beijing. A judgement that political warfare has failed is the most plausible route from the current equilibrium to a coercive one; the drone-bill blocking campaign and the Beidaihe objective of electing 'patriotic forces' in 2026 suggest Beijing currently believes that track is working
update_triggers: Revise UP sharply if the PRC announces or executes a shipping quarantine, customs-inspection regime or closure area around Taiwan lasting beyond 72 hours, or if a commercial vessel bound for Taiwan is boarded, diverted or detained under Coast Guard Order No. 3. The baseline since June 2026 is radio hailing and interrogation without boarding, so boarding is the threshold crossing; a requirement that vessels report through China's International Trade Single Window, the first rung on the ladder Taiwan war-gamed on 25 June, would be the earliest warning

Revise UP if the PLA announces a new named exercise on the Joint Sword, Strait Thunder or Justice Mission pattern with no announced end date, if a Fujian MSA navigation warning covers waters beyond the 12km coastal band, or if MND daily sorties recover above 40 with median-line crossings sustained for a week or more once Typhoon Saudel clears. A sharp recovery from the current floor would be more informative than the floor itself

Revise UP if Theodore Roosevelt is confirmed to CENTCOM in September with no Pacific replacement assigned, if a third carrier is committed to CENTCOM, or if PLA surface action groups or the Fujian carrier begin operating east of Taiwan while no US carrier is present in PACOM. forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 1 to 1. The 80% interval stays at [0, 1]. Today the single largest resolvable input in this question stopped being a forecast and became a published fact, and it landed almost exactly where the analyst community had put it.

Ofgem confirmed the Default Tariff Cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 at around 7am this morning. The new level is GBP 1,723 a year for a typical dual-fuel direct debit household, a rise of roughly GBP 60, or 3.6%, from the current GBP 1,663. Cornwall Insight's final forecast on 19 August was GBP 1,729.31, or 4.0%; Uswitch reported suppliers converging on about 3.7% after the observation window closed on 19 August. So the outcome came in a touch below consensus, but only by about GBP 6, four tenths of a percentage point on the quarterly change. Neither of yesterday's thresholds fired. I said I would revise up if the cap came in at or below GBP 1,663, which would have removed the administered impulse entirely, and down to zero if it came in at or above GBP 1,747. It did neither, so the arithmetic of the question is unchanged: the cap covering the October, November and December reference months, which is three of the four publishable attempts left, rises rather than falls, and it does so despite the removal of the 5% VAT rate on domestic electricity from 1 October. Martin Lewis's team make the point that from 1 October electricity unit rates under the cap will be restated without VAT, so the headline unit rate will look lower than today's even though the underlying wholesale-driven cost has gone up. That restatement is a genuine CPI-relevant price cut for consumers, because CPI prices goods inclusive of VAT, and on an electricity weight of roughly two and a half per cent a 4.8% reduction is worth on the order of a tenth of a point on the index. But it is already inside the 3.6% headline, already inside every published forecast, and nowhere near the roughly one full percentage point of unexpected disinflation this question requires.

The genuinely new information today came from crude, and it is the largest YES-friendly move I have recorded in this series. Brent ended Tuesday 25 August near USD 87.12 and WTI at USD 82.36, against Monday's close of USD 92.17 and USD 85.01. That is a fall of USD 7.27, or 7.7%, from Friday's close, across two sessions. Trading Economics had Brent as low as USD 86.33 intraday, down 6.33% on the day. Two things did it, and both point the same way. First, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's Operation Economic Outcast, unveiled Monday with Normandy imagery and around sixty designations covering digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, set no deadline for secondary sanctions and designated no major Chinese bank, and China takes well over eighty per cent of Iran's seaborne crude. Bessent called it a warning shot. Second, Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spent Monday in Tehran carrying a reported sanctions-relief proposal, meeting President Pezeshkian, negotiator Ghalibaf and General Rezaei, while Oman's foreign minister worked separately on navigation rules for the strait and word circulated that Washington might return evacuated diplomats. The cleanest read is the Murban spread: Abu Dhabi's light grade leaves via the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline and never enters Hormuz, and its premium over Brent, north of USD 11 on Monday, roughly halved by Tuesday afternoon. That is a war premium coming out of the price, and it is coming out fastest where it was thickest. The EIA's August outlook has Brent averaging USD 85 in Q3, USD 78 in Q4 and USD 69 across 2027.

I have taken that seriously and it still does not move the number, for four reasons. First, the physical floor has not moved. Hormuz throughput fell from 21.6 million barrels a day in Q4 2025 to 4.9 million a day in Q2 2026, shut-in production averaged 5.5 million a day in July, global inventories drew 4.2 million a day in Q2 and the EIA projects a further 3.8 million a day this quarter. Not one barrel was released by either Monday's sanctions or Munir's visit; what was removed was fear. Second, the framework Munir invoked, the Islamabad memorandum signed on 17 June, saw its sixty-day window lapse in the middle of this month with neither side extending, and Rezaei and Ghalibaf both told him Washington must move first. A 7.7% repricing resting on an expired framework is exactly the kind of move that reverses. Third, and most important for this question, transmission from crude to consumer prices is currently broken downstream. The US diesel crack touched a record USD 102.20 a barrel on 17 August and is still near USD 100, distillate stocks were around 107.1 million barrels in early August, the thinnest for the time of year since 1996, and US retail diesel rose fifteen cents in the same week that Brent fell 7.7%. When the binding constraint is refining capacity rather than crude, cheaper Brent does not reach the pump, and motor fuels carry only about three per cent of the UK CPI basket in any case. Fourth, the UK-relevant energy price is gas, not oil, and gas barely budged: NBP settled at 163 pence per therm on 25 August, down 3.6% on the day but off a 169 pence high that is the strongest since January 2023, while TTF held above EUR 68 per megawatt hour, also the highest since January 2023, with EU storage around 55% at end-July, some eleven points below a year earlier, and hot weather slowing injections.

One technical item worth logging. ONS confirms it has not been able to update to 2026 CPI and CPIH weights in line with standard methodology because of delays in processing the underlying household final consumption expenditure survey data and the need for further quality assurance; the series is running on 2025 weights and ONS will update when the data allow. A mid-series reweighting is the kind of technical event that can shift a headline print, and it is the sort of thing that keeps me at 1 rather than 0. Historically, though, weight updates move the annual rate by hundredths, occasionally a tenth. They do not deliver a hundred basis points.

The forecaster distribution is untouched. The Bank of England's July Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking around 3.2% in Q4 2026 with risks tilted to the upside; Pill, Greene and Mann voted for 4.00% at the end of July; a Reuters poll conducted 13 to 18 August found 56 of 64 economists expecting Bank Rate held at 3.75% for the rest of the year and none expecting a change on 17 September, with markets still assigning some probability to a hike rather than a cut. HM Treasury's August comparison of independent forecasts averages 3.4% for Q4 2026, and Deutsche Bank sees the peak at 3.3% to 3.5%. Nobody published has an in-window month near 2.0%.

So: the biggest uncertainty in the window resolved, marginally on the friendly side of consensus but still upward; the biggest disinflationary impulse of the series arrived in crude but is blocked downstream and does not touch the administered gas and electricity prices that dominate the remaining reference months. Those roughly cancel. Four attempts remain, August published 16 September, September 21 October, October 18 November and November 16 December, with December 2026 publishing 20 January 2027 and therefore mechanically outside. I hold at 1.
forecasts.base_rate:
The primary reference class is the historical frequency with which UK CPI annual inflation, having printed in the 2.7% to 3.1% band, subsequently printed below 2.0% within four months. Using ONS CPI back to 1989, months in that band number in the low hundreds, and the share followed within four months by a sub-2.0% reading is on the order of 5% to 8%. That is the raw outside view, and it flatters the YES case here for three structural reasons.

First, every episode that actually delivered a full percentage point of disinflation in four months was driven by a sharp negative energy shock, a tax cut or a demand collapse, not by gradual services cooling. The clearest cases are 2008-09, when the financial crisis coincided with a temporary VAT cut to 15%; 2014-15, when oil roughly halved and CPI fell from about 1.6% to zero over eight months; and 2020, when the pandemic combined with VAT reductions and Eat Out to Help Out to compress the index. In each the impulse ran the opposite way to today. As of 26 August 2026 Ofgem has confirmed the October to December cap at GBP 1,723, up 3.6% from GBP 1,663 and rising even after the removal of VAT on domestic electricity; NBP gas is at 163 pence per therm, off a 169 pence high that is the strongest since January 2023; TTF is above EUR 68 per megawatt hour, also the highest since January 2023; and EU storage was around 55% at the end of July, roughly eleven points below the prior year. Conditioning the reference class on a rising rather than falling administered energy impulse cuts the historical hit rate close to zero. I cannot identify a single UK episode in the inflation-targeting era in which CPI fell from near 3% to below 2% within four months while regulated energy prices were increasing.

Second, the naive class ignores the publication constraint, which is the binding feature here. The ONS release page for Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026 gives a release date of 20 January 2027, so the December reference month cannot resolve this question. The window closes with the November data on 16 December 2026 and contains exactly four attempts: August, published 16 September; September, published 21 October; October, published 18 November; and November, published 16 December. Those are not independent draws at a 5% to 8% hazard. They share the same energy base, the same administered cap across October to December, and the same services momentum, so the right structure is closer to one correlated draw at a low probability. Multiplying four monthly hazards would badly overstate the answer.

Third, a forecast-error reference class provides an independent check. The distribution of Bank of England four-quarter-ahead CPI forecast errors has a standard deviation of roughly 1.0 to 1.3 percentage points over the past two decades, but the large errors cluster in shock years and have recently been almost entirely on the upside. The Bank's July 2026 MPR central path has CPI at about 3.2% in Q4 2026 with risks tilted up. A sub-2.0% print inside the window requires an error of roughly 1.3 percentage points in the disinflationary direction at a horizon of two to four months, not four quarters. Over horizons that short the standard deviation of CPI errors is far smaller, on the order of 0.2 to 0.4 percentage points, because energy, food and administered components are largely already observable. With the October-to-December cap now published rather than forecast, that observability is stronger today than it was yesterday. A 1.3 percentage point downside miss at a three-month horizon is a three-to-five sigma event on that distribution. That framing is what stops me drifting upward on genuinely encouraging food and services data: CPI food and non-alcoholic beverages at 1.3% in the twelve months to July 2026, the lowest since September 2021, with BRC reporting intense grocery competition, and services down to 3.4% from 4.4% in January, are real improvements but nowhere near sufficient.

The cross-forecaster distribution says the same. HM Treasury's August 2026 comparison of independent forecasts averages 3.4% for Q4 2026, down from 3.7% in June; the Bank has about 3.2%; Deutsche Bank puts the peak at 3.3% to 3.5%. A Reuters poll conducted 13 to 18 August found 56 of 64 economists expecting Bank Rate held at 3.75% through year end and none expecting a change on 17 September, with markets still pricing some chance of a hike. That is not the configuration you observe when the consensus thinks inflation is about to undershoot the target by a percentage point. When the entire published distribution sits more than a percentage point above the threshold and dispersion between forecasters is only a few tenths, the implied probability of a crossing is small before any energy-direction adjustment.

An index-arithmetic sanity check on the friendliest month. The October 2025 CPI index rose 0.4% on the month to 139.8, which makes October 2026 the least demanding of the four remaining base comparisons: a 1.9% print requires the index at about 142.5, a cumulative fall of roughly 0.27% from July 2026's 142.9. That is not enormous in the abstract, but it has to be delivered across three months in which the confirmed Ofgem cap rises 3.6% and housing and household services, which went from 2.7% to 4.1% in July on the back of the 13% July cap increase, is contributing upward.

A reference class on the oil transmission channel is also worth carrying, because today's crude move is the largest disinflationary news of the series. Historically, a sustained 20% fall in sterling crude prices removes something like 0.3 to 0.4 percentage points from UK CPI via motor fuels over three to six months, given a fuels and lubricants weight near three per cent. Brent at USD 87.12 is about 7.7% below Friday's close but still roughly 30% above a year ago, so the year-on-year fuels contribution remains positive. And the current episode has an unusual blockage: the US diesel crack hit a record USD 102.20 a barrel on 17 August with distillate stocks the thinnest for the time of year since 1996, so retail fuel is not tracking crude at all. The historical pass-through coefficient is, if anything, an overestimate right now.

Finally, a calibration note on the counterfactual. The House of Commons Library records that before the Middle East conflict, UK CPI had been expected to fall to around 2% from April 2026 and stay near 2% for the rest of the year, and the Bank said the same in its pre-conflict projections. Absent the war this would be close to a coin flip. With the war, and with its price effects now locked into a published administered cap covering three of the four in-scope reference months, it is not. Combining: the band-based class gives 5% to 8%; conditioning on a rising energy impulse cuts that by roughly an order of magnitude; the publication constraint removes two of the calendar months a casual reading assumes; and the short-horizon forecast-error distribution puts the required miss at three or more sigma. That converges on 1%.

forecasts.question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 100 to 100. I hold at the ceiling for a seventeenth consecutive day, and today is the cleanest single day of evidence in this entire series: both named resolution sources refreshed overnight, both moved upward, and both now agree to the dollar on the domestic line for a second consecutive day.

Verification performed today, Wednesday 26 August 2026 at 08:07:15 UTC, by direct raw-HTML request with a desktop browser user-agent, compression enabled and redirects followed. Box Office Mojo (https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl2299756545/) returned HTTP 200, 177,644 bytes on disk, MD5 e4d74e535a9346273b8e4ccff3cf9303, and reports Domestic $858,400,177 (38.6 per cent), International $1,365,000,000 (61.4 per cent) and Worldwide $2,223,400,177, with opening weekend unchanged at $360,091,572 across 4,487 theatres and a release date of 31 July 2026. The Numbers (https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/Spider-Man-Brand-New-Day-(2026)) returned HTTP 200, 138,733 bytes, MD5 0a234229795d42739b74676bc04b0cbf, and reports Domestic Box Office $858,400,177, International Box Office $1,366,115,336 explicitly datestamped 8/26/2026, and Worldwide Box Office $2,224,515,513, alongside Legs of 2.38 and a domestic share of 38.6 per cent. Both worldwide lines reconcile exactly against their own published components: 858,400,177 + 1,365,000,000 = 2,223,400,177, and 858,400,177 + 1,366,115,336 = 2,224,515,513. Taking the LOWER of the two, as I have throughout, the film stands at $2,223,400,177 worldwide. That is 48.2 per cent above the $1.5B threshold, a buffer of $723,400,177, up $3,498,996 on yesterday's buffer.

The day's movement is entirely upward and entirely on the domestic line. Both sources moved from $854,901,181 to $858,400,177, a gain of $3,498,996, which is a plausible Monday-plus-Tuesday actuals ingestion for a film running roughly $3.5M to $4.5M per weekday in its fourth and fifth weeks. Critically, they moved in lockstep and landed on the identical figure to the dollar. Yesterday I flagged as an open question whether the newly exact domestic agreement reflected genuine independent ingestion of the same Comscore actual or one source mirroring the other. Today's evidence leans toward the former for a specific reason: the two sources moved together on domestic but did NOT move together on international, where Box Office Mojo held its round $1,365,000,000 for a third consecutive day while The Numbers held $1,366,115,336 for a second. If The Numbers were simply mirroring Box Office Mojo's feed, the international lines would have converged too. They have not. The feeds are independent; they simply happen to draw domestic from the same reconciled Comscore actual, which is exactly what one would expect and exactly what makes the corroboration meaningful rather than illusory.

The international divergence is therefore stable at $1,115,336, identical to yesterday, rather than growing. Box Office Mojo's flat round number is the signature of a studio-reported international estimate awaiting reconciliation, and it has now been static for three days while the domestic line updated twice. That is a mild staleness on one field of one source, worth noting but not worth a single basis point: it is 0.05 per cent of the cume and 0.15 per cent of the buffer, and the direction of any eventual catch-up is upward, not downward.

External corroboration strengthened materially today. The Hollywood Reporter reports the film has hit No. 2 on the all-time domestic chart, topping Avengers: Endgame, which independently confirms a domestic cume in the $858M region since Endgame's final domestic sits at $858.4M. Forbes on 24 August reported the film passing both Titanic and Ne Zha 2 to become the fourth-biggest film ever worldwide, with subsequent coverage placing it at $2.224 billion and closing on Avatar: The Way of Water at No. 3, less than $100M ahead. That is three independent trade outlets, none of them a named resolution source, all placing the worldwide cume within a rounding error of the two aggregator figures I retrieved directly. When Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Forbes, the Washington Post, Box Office Mojo and The Numbers all place a number in the same $2.22B to $2.23B band, the probability that all seven are wrong by the $723M required to threaten this threshold is not a number I can meaningfully write down.

I also re-ran a targeted search for any correction, re-audit or restatement notice covering this title from Box Office Mojo, The Numbers, Comscore or Sony. Null for a third consecutive day. The only revisions in the published record remain the well-documented upward ones from opening: first Friday including previews restated to $169.8M, the domestic opening weekend from a Sunday estimate of $355M to a final $360,091,572, and the global opening from $927M to $932M. Not one downward restatement of any magnitude exists in this film's entire published history. That directional asymmetry is the single most important structural fact here, because the only mechanism producing a NO is a large, durable, correlated downward restatement, and the empirical record on this title contains zero instances of downward restatement at any size.

Retrieval also improved today. Yesterday's first curl attempt returned HTTP 200 with a zero-byte body and needed a retry. Today both fetches succeeded on the first attempt with full bodies. That does not eliminate instrument risk, which has recurred on 19, 22, 23, 24 and 25 August, but it is the first clean single-pass retrieval of the series and it slightly reduces my concern about a resolution-day fetch failure.

For a NO, both named sources would have to restate the worldwide cume downward by more than $723,400,177, or 32.5 per cent of the lower published figure, simultaneously, and hold that restatement through 31 December. With 127 days to run, a film still in wide release, and a cumulative-by-then rather than snapshot test, the buffer can only widen. I hold central at 100.

I keep the lower CI bound at 99 rather than closing to 100, for reasons unchanged and unrelated to box office. Residual risk is now almost entirely instrument and adjudication risk: the 23 August episode proved a named source can display a materially wrong nine-figure value for a full day with no correction notice, retrieval has failed on five of the last eight days before retry, and resolver mechanics remain unobservable to me. A 1-point floor is the honest price of that residual. Seventeen days of confirmation should not persuade me that a published number is a law of nature.
forecasts.base_rate:
The naive outside view for this question is the class "wide-release tentpole films that reach $1.5B worldwide". Fewer than fifteen titles in cinema history have done it, and the unconditional base rate for any given tentpole entering production is low single digits. That was the right frame in June 2026, before release, and a disciplined forecaster starting from scratch then should have sat somewhere in the 20 to 40 per cent range for a Spider-Man sequel with this cast and this release date. Applying that class today would be a textbook base-rate error of exactly the kind superforecasting discipline exists to prevent: choosing a reference class that discards the single most informative conditioning fact available, namely that the event has already happened, happened in the film's second week of release, and is published on both named resolution sources in close agreement and corroborated by at least five independent trade outlets.

The governing reference class today is narrower and stranger: "published cumulative box office figures on a major aggregator that are subsequently restated below a milestone the film had already cleared, and stay restated". Framed that way the question is not about ticket sales at all. Nobody is forecasting future demand. The forecast is about the stability of an already-published, independently corroborated accounting figure over a 127-day horizon.

The historical rate of that outcome, at the magnitude required here, is effectively zero. Aggregators revise constantly, but the revisions have a strong and well-documented signature: they are small, they are overwhelmingly upward, and they cluster in the narrow window where Sunday weekend estimates convert to Monday actuals. This film's own revision history is a textbook instance. Every documented restatement on Brand New Day has been upward: first Friday including previews to $169.8M, domestic opening weekend from a $355M Sunday estimate to a $360,091,572 final, global opening from $927M to $932M, and today's ordinary $3,498,996 domestic accretion as weekday actuals were ingested. Not one downward revision of any size appears anywhere in this title's published record. The 23 August episode, which briefly looked like a $252.5M downward restatement on Box Office Mojo's international line, reversed upward within twenty-four hours and is firmly diagnosed as a stale field carrying a five-day-old value for a single day.

So the relevant population is not "aggregators sometimes print lower numbers", which they do transiently, but "aggregators durably restate a reported worldwide cume down by roughly a third, on two independently maintained databases at once, and hold it for four months". I am aware of no modern case. The restatement required is $723,400,177, or 32.5 per cent of the lower published figure. Scaling from a three per cent maximum observed correction to a thirty-two per cent required correction is a ten-fold extrapolation beyond the tail of the observed distribution.

A second relevant class is "forecasting questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied and publicly reported months before the deadline". These resolve as expected at a rate indistinguishable from one. The residual failure modes in that class are procedural rather than empirical: the question is voided or reworded, the resolver consults a source other than the two named, the resolver reads the wording idiosyncratically, or both named sources become unavailable at the moment of adjudication. The wording here is unusually forgiving on each count. "Gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026" is a cumulative-by-then test rather than a snapshot test, so the film leaving theatres cannot reduce the resolving figure. It names two sources joined by "or", so either satisfying the criterion suffices. Both currently satisfy it by wide margins and agree to the dollar on domestic.

I weight the second and third classes most heavily and the naive pre-release class at essentially zero, since conditioning on realised outcomes strictly dominates. The dominant residual risk is not box office: it is resolver mechanics, question administration, and measurement error at the point of adjudication. That is why the central estimate sits at the reporting ceiling while the lower bound of the interval does not.

forecasts.base_rate:
The governing reference class is not "will two firms grow into a threshold" but "a threshold is already exceeded on the public record by roughly 50%, four months before the measurement date, in a domain with a monotonic underlying trend; will it still be exceeded then". That is a persistence question, and persistence questions of this structure resolve YES at very high rates. On public forecasting platforms, questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied by a wide margin, with no identified mechanism for reversal, resolve YES in the high nineties. The correct anchor is 97-99%, and the residual is dominated by resolution mechanics rather than by the world changing.

Five narrower classes point the same way.

First, revenue trajectories of large private technology companies at $10bn-plus scale. Documented instances of a firm's disclosed annualised revenue falling more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or an exogenous demand collapse, are close to unrepresented. The available cases are Wirecard and FTX, where revenue was substantially fictitious, and the 2020 travel and hospitality shock, where the demand base physically disappeared. Neither template fits: Anthropic's Q2 revenue is cash-collected and carries positive adjusted operating income, and enterprise seat counts and API volumes are growing rather than vanishing. To fail, the combined figure would need to fall roughly a third from $105bn, which has no precedent at this scale outside accounting fraud.

Second, "leaked or reported private-company run rate later revised downward". This class is not empty. Figures sourced from investor decks and internal memos have historically been revised by 10-30% when audited financials appear, and the gross-versus-net principal-agent question under ASC 606 is exactly the kind of issue that produces such a revision. The generic base rate for a material downward restatement at IPO for a company with a contested revenue-recognition policy is perhaps 15-25%. The specific market pricing available on this case is more favourable: roughly 50% SEC affirmation of gross treatment, 40% a requirement for disaggregated disclosure, 10% actual restatement. Disaggregated disclosure is neutral-to-helpful, since it would let a resolver see both gross and net and both clear on Q4 data. What sharply cuts this class further is a new observation: independent alternative-data trackers (TickerTrends $74.1bn, Yipit $74.3bn) estimate Anthropic ABOVE its own reported $65bn, and SemiAnalysis's bottom-up model corroborates roughly $100bn combined. When third-party reconstruction lands above the company figure rather than below, the prior on the company figure being inflated should fall, not rise.

Third, "definitional ambiguity in a resolution criterion turns an apparently-cleared question into a dispute". This remains the largest single residual. Three conventions are live: exit-month annualised run rate (about $105bn reported, $115bn on trackers), a net-basis adjustment of Anthropic (about $97bn on OpenAI's own $8bn allegation), and trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised (about $73.2bn on stale Q2 data). Questions relying on a metric that companies define inconsistently generate disputes at rates in the 5-15% range. What pulls this down sharply is that all three conventions clear today, and projected to Q4 all three clear with room. Anthropic's Q1-to-Q2 sequential growth was about 145%; even heavily damped, Q4 recognised revenue lands in the $20-35bn range, annualising to $80-140bn on Anthropic alone.

Fourth, "sector-wide financing shock disrupts a leading private firm's operations within four months". AI equities have drawn down hard and Nvidia reports today, 26 August, after seven consecutive down sessions. But in the 2000-2002 and 2008-2009 analogues, revenue at firms with contracted enterprise commitments fell over years, not months, and typically by 10-25% rather than 33%. Within four months, the probability that a financing shock cuts reported run rate by a third is well under 1%.

Fifth, "price war compresses realised revenue at a fast-growing usage-based software firm". The empirical record in cloud and AI inference is that unit-price declines of 20-80% have been repeatedly absorbed by volume growth, with reported revenue continuing to rise. Prices for equivalent capability have fallen 90-97% across 2025-26 while both firms' revenue grew by multiples. For the price war to produce a NO here, elasticity would have to invert abruptly, with volume flat or falling while prices drop a third. There is no instance of that in this sector at this stage of adoption.

One class deserves fresh weight: "reported growth decelerates faster than expected". This is now empirically live, with Anthropic's month-on-month growth down from roughly 55% in spring to mid-single digits in July on tracker data. But deceleration is a growth-rate story and this question is a level question. Even at zero further growth the combined figure sits 50% above the bar; at zero growth for Anthropic alone the trackers still put it at $74bn, above the combined threshold.

Aggregating: persistence anchor 98-99%, minus under 1pp for the combined restatement-plus-adversarial-convention branch, minus a few tenths for demand collapse, price-war and financing-shock paths, minus a small allowance for the resolver failing to find or agree on Q4 figures. That lands at 98.5-99. I take 99, with the floor at 98 to acknowledge that the ASC 606 branch remains formally open until the public S-1 lands and that the two legs will be measured on different evidentiary bases.
