forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 36 to 35. A one-point trim. Today's information flow contains one genuinely clarifying upward anchor that I had not previously recorded and three modest downward corrections to factors I credited over the past 48 hours, and on balance the corrections outweigh the anchor slightly. The discipline after Sunday's three-point move is to test that move rather than extend it, and testing it today produced more friction than support.

The upward anchor first, because it is the most important thing I found and because it partly rescues my central estimate from drifting lower. The OBR's Fiscal risks and sustainability report, published 7 July 2026 and launched at the Darlington Economic Campus, sets a baseline scenario assuming long-term average productivity growth of 1.4 per cent over the next fifty years which, combined with projected changes in the workforce, implies real GDP growth averaging around one and a half per cent a year across the long run. For the first time the OBR has incorporated an explicit projection of the capital stock, so it now decomposes long-run productivity into capital deepening and total factor productivity rather than assuming a single trend. That is the official long-run anchor for exactly the variable this question resolves on, and it sits at the threshold rather than beneath it. I had been carrying the medium-term EFO numbers as my institutional anchor, where TFP growth reaches only 0.8 per cent in 2030 and potential output growth is around 1.4 to 1.5 per cent, and I had implicitly assumed the long-run projection would be lower still. It is not. The FRS also runs a higher-productivity scenario with TFP at 1.3 per cent a year, 0.3 points above baseline, which the OBR says would cut borrowing by around 50 billion pounds in 2030-31 and push the point at which debt turns unsustainable back nearly twenty years, and a downside scenario in which productivity growth remains at 0.5 per cent, close to its post-financial-crisis average. The existence of a named, quantified downside scenario at 0.5 per cent is itself informative about where the OBR thinks the risk lies.

I do not treat the FRS baseline as implying a fifty per cent probability, and the reason is the shape of the path. The OBR's medium-term forecast has TFP still climbing towards 0.8 per cent in 2030; the 1.4 per cent long-run figure is a convergence assumption reached over subsequent decades. The 2030s are the earliest and therefore the lowest slice of that fifty-year window. Under the OBR's own baseline the decade mean for 2030-2039 is very plausibly 1.3 to 1.4 per cent, not 1.5. So the FRS confirms my central estimate rather than overturning it, and it is a reason to nudge the upper tail of my distribution rather than the central case.

Now the corrections. The first is Andrew Bailey's Mansion House speech of 14 July 2026, which I had cited only through the Monetary Policy Report's quarterly potential-supply figure of 0.3 to 0.4 per cent. Read directly, Bailey decomposes the record: for roughly fifteen years before the financial crisis, UK potential supply grew at around 2.8 per cent a year, of which productivity contributed 2.4 points and labour supply 0.4 points; for the fifteen years since the crisis, potential growth has fallen to 1.3 per cent, of which productivity contributed just 0.4 points and labour supply 0.8 points. That composition is the whole argument in one line. The post-crisis UK bought two thirds of its potential growth from labour supply, and labour supply is precisely the component that ONS demographics take away in the 2030s. Yesterday I credited the Bank's potential-supply estimate as straddling the 1.5 per cent bar. Bailey's own framing puts the Bank's recent-history number at 1.3 per cent, below the bar, with the productivity leg at 0.4 points. To clear 1.5 per cent through the 2030s the productivity contribution has to more than triple from its post-crisis average while the labour contribution roughly halves. That is a harder ask than the quarterly figure alone implied, and I mark down my Bank-of-England factor accordingly.

The second correction concerns business investment, where I gave two points on Monday for the ONS provisional Q2 2026 estimate showing a 1.7 per cent quarterly rise. The EY UK Economic Outlook published this month forecasts UK GDP growth of 0.9 per cent in 2026, up from 0.8 per cent in May, but simultaneously downgrades business investment to a fall of 0.7 per cent across 2026, against the zero growth forecast in May, citing energy costs and inflation staying higher for longer. It has investment returning to growth only in 2027 and 2028, at a downgraded 1.8 and 2.6 per cent, and unemployment rising to 5.3 per cent by end-2026 before easing to 5.1 and then 4.8 per cent in 2028. EY also warns explicitly that the UK faces recession if the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz lasts into 2027, which would cut 2026 growth to 0.5 per cent and shrink the economy 0.2 per cent next year. A forecaster looking at the same Q2 print and still marking down the annual investment path is telling me my two-point credit was too generous for one provisional, bias-adjusted quarter. I keep the factor but shrink it.

The third is subtler and cuts at the foundation of the bull case. The ONS labour market transformation update published this month reports that Labour Force Survey response levels have improved markedly since 2023 following higher incentives and more interviewers, with waves two to five slightly above their pre-pandemic level in January to March 2026, and that the Transformed Labour Force Survey is on track to become the headline measure in 2027. The entire Resolution Foundation and CEP LSE case rests on the LFS denominator being broken. If the LFS is convalescing, the wedge between the survey-based and administrative-data productivity measures should narrow over time, and it is not obvious in which direction. The ONS separately acknowledges it needs to give a clearer steer on which productivity measure to use, which is a fair admission but not a resolution.

Two smaller items lean up and I record them without moving on them. The Resolution Foundation's Q3 2026 Macroeconomic Policy Outlook notes that the 1.1 per cent annual growth in output per hour over the two years to Q2 2026 is faster than the 0.7 per cent rate of the late 2010s, and the Retail Gazette coverage of 24 August confirms retail is among the twelve of nineteen sectors recording gains, which speaks directly to my trigger about the pickup spreading beyond information and communication into large-employment sectors. But note what the bull number actually delivers if projected forward: 1.1 per cent productivity plus 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input gives 1.3 to 1.6 per cent, centred at about 1.4. Even the optimists' measure, taken at face value and held for a decade, lands just short of the bar. The same Outlook records that ONS output per hour in Q2 2026 is around 5 per cent below the level implied by the OBR's final pre-Covid forecast, roughly 150 billion pounds a year or 4,500 pounds per worker. Separately, analysts now expect gilt yields to fall ahead of the 28 October Budget, potentially restoring the 10 to 12 billion pounds of headroom lost this year, which marginally eases the risk that public capital spending is cut to meet the fiscal rules.

Mechanically I hold the decade mean at roughly 1.30 to 1.35 per cent with a standard deviation near 0.5 points, shading the point estimate a touch down within that range on the Bailey decomposition. That gives 34 to 36 per cent. I take 35. The scheduled events that should move this are unchanged: the quarterly national accounts and revised Q2 business investment on 30 September, the ONS productivity methods article due September, the Healey Budget and OBR EFO on 28 October, the Blue Book revisions article on 30 October, the November Monetary Policy Report and the Q3 productivity flash on 17 November.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is UK decade averages of annual real GDP growth as the ONS reports them, on the post-Blue Book 2026 vintage published 20 August 2026, because the question resolves on the ONS-reported arithmetic mean of ten annual growth rates.

Decade averages run roughly: 1950s 2.6 per cent; 1960s 3.1 per cent; 1970s 2.4 per cent; 1980s 2.7 per cent; 1990s 2.2 per cent; 2000s 1.8 per cent including the 4.5 per cent contraction in 2009; and 2010-2019 now 2.1 per cent on the revised vintage. Seven completed decades, seven above 1.5 per cent. The 2020s are the outlier: 2020 minus 10.3, 2021 plus 8.6, 2022 plus 4.8, 2023 about plus 0.5 revised, 2024 plus 1.1 revised, 2025 about plus 1.4, and 2026 tracking near 0.9 to 1.1 per cent on the August HM Treasury consensus and the EY Economic Outlook. That is a seven-year mean near 0.8 per cent and roughly 1.0 to 1.2 per cent across 2023-2026.

I do not use the naive seven-for-seven frequency as my anchor. Seven decade averages from one country are not seven independent draws; they are one heavily serially correlated series with a large standard error, drawn overwhelmingly from a growth regime that no longer exists. A rising working-age share, technological catch-up to the US frontier, expanding female participation, financial deepening and progressive integration into the European single market each did real work in those decades, and each has exhausted itself or reversed. Andrew Bailey put the structural break in numbers at Mansion House on 14 July 2026: for roughly fifteen years before the financial crisis, UK potential supply grew around 2.8 per cent a year, with productivity contributing 2.4 points and labour supply 0.4 points; for the fifteen years since, potential growth has been 1.3 per cent, with productivity contributing 0.4 points and labour supply 0.8 points. Treating the pre-crisis record as a frequency count would be a textbook reference-class error.

The disciplined approach is decomposition. Decade real GDP growth equals growth in labour input plus growth in output per hour. On labour input, the ONS 2024-based national population projections published in April 2026 have the UK population rising from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million by mid-2034, growth of 1.7 million or 2.5 per cent over ten years, with all of it from net international migration. Working-age population rises from 44.3 million to 45.8 million, about 0.33 per cent a year, natural change turns negative from mid-2026, and the pensionable-age population rises 14.6 per cent. Net migration was 171,000 in the year to December 2025, down from 331,000, is projected at 138,000 in 2026, and is assumed to stabilise near 230,000 thereafter. Hours per worker have trended down for decades. Labour input therefore realistically contributes 0.2 to 0.5 points a year through the 2030s, against roughly 0.8 to 1.1 points in the post-crisis period.

That leaves productivity needing about 1.0 to 1.3 points a year, sustained for ten years, for YES. What is it delivering? This is where the reference class dissolves into a measurement dispute. On the ONS LFS-based measure, output per hour was minus 0.2 per cent year on year in Q2 2026 and just 2.3 per cent above its 2019 average. On the ONS RTI-based measure the ONS has preferred since June 2026, plus 0.7 per cent year on year and 4.6 per cent above 2019, with a minus 0.8 per cent quarterly fall in Q2 after an upwardly revised plus 1.1 per cent in Q1. On the Resolution Foundation's administrative-data measure of 24 August 2026, 1.1 per cent a year since Q3 2024, faster than the 0.7 per cent of the late 2010s, after a 0.7 per cent annual fall over the two prior years. On the CEP LSE baseline in Occasional Paper 74, roughly 1.6 per cent annualised. On Morgan Stanley's private-sector estimate, 1.8 per cent a year. Pre-crisis, 1997-2007, whole-economy productivity ran near 2 per cent. Credible estimates for the same economy over the same window span more than a full percentage point, and that dispersion is the honest summary of the state of knowledge.

On forecast track records the outside view is bearish, though less uniformly than I had it. The OBR has revised its medium-term productivity assumption down repeatedly since 2010; in November 2025 it cut underlying medium-term TFP growth from 1.1 to 0.8 per cent, taking 2029 potential output growth to 1.5 per cent from 1.8 per cent, with capital deepening at 0.2 and labour supply at 0.5, and the March 2026 EFO left TFP unchanged, reaching 0.8 per cent in 2030. Against that, the OBR's Fiscal risks and sustainability report of 7 July 2026 sets a fifty-year baseline of 1.4 per cent productivity growth implying real GDP growth of around one and a half per cent a year, with a higher-productivity scenario at 1.3 per cent TFP and a downside at 0.5 per cent. The IMF's 2026 Article IV, concluded 16 July 2026, puts potential near 1.4 per cent. NIESR's trend estimate is 1.25 per cent, with growth of 1.4 per cent in 2026 moderating to 1.3 per cent in 2027 and settling around 1.3 to 1.4 per cent thereafter. The OBR's Briefing Paper No. 9 has AI adding around 0.2 percentage points to annual productivity growth by the forecast horizon, and the Penn Wharton Budget Model has the AI contribution peaking near 0.2 points in the early 2030s before fading to a permanent 0.04 points. Note that the institutional central cases cluster tightly at 1.25 to 1.5 per cent, which is why this question is a genuine forecast rather than a formality.

Two asymmetries lean up. First, ONS revision bias: Blue Book 2026 showed a mean plus 0.06 point revision to annual volume growth across 1998-2024, with cumulative 1997-2024 volume growth revised from 59.2 to 61.7 per cent and the 2010-2019 decade average revised up 0.1 point to 2.1 per cent. Since the question resolves on ONS-reported figures, this is a real thumb on the scale. Second, output-gap arithmetic: a downturn before 2030 with recovery growth landing inside the window would flatter the decade mean by 0.4 to 0.6 points. Netting these against a decomposed central estimate of roughly 1.30 to 1.35 per cent with a standard deviation near 0.5 points gives 34 to 36 per cent. Anchor: 35.
factors_up: OBR Fiscal risks and sustainability report, 7 July 2026: fifty-year baseline assumes long-term average productivity growth of 1.4 per cent which, combined with projected workforce changes, implies real GDP growth averaging around one and a half per cent a year, with a higher-productivity scenario at 1.3 per cent TFP cutting borrowing by 50 billion pounds in 2030-31. The official long-run anchor for the resolution variable sits at the threshold, not beneath it, and for the first time incorporates an explicit capital-stock projection. (+6pp)

Resolution Foundation report of 24 August 2026 and the Q3 2026 Macroeconomic Policy Outlook: output per hour growing 1.1 per cent a year over the two years to Q2 2026 on HMRC RTI payroll and self-assessment data, against a 0.7 per cent annual decline in the two prior years and faster than the 0.7 per cent rate of the late 2010s. Broad-based across 12 of 19 major sectors and driven within sectors rather than by composition, with retail among the gainers per Retail Gazette on 24 August. (+6pp)

Independent corroboration of the measurement case: CEP LSE Occasional Paper 74 (Barbas, Valero, Van Reenen, July 2026) finds output per worker up 0.3 per cent on the LFS basis between 2024 Q3 and 2026 Q1 against 2.4 per cent on its preferred RTI-plus-HMRC baseline, roughly 1.6 per cent annualised; Morgan Stanley's Bruna Skarica has private-sector productivity at 1.8 per cent a year. The ONS itself switched its recommended measure to tax data in June 2026. (+4pp)

Blue Book 2026 (ONS, 20 August 2026) confirms persistent upward revision bias in ONS-reported real growth, the exact metric this question resolves on: mean revision plus 0.06 percentage points a year across 1998-2024, cumulative 1997-2024 volume growth revised from 59.2 to 61.7 per cent, and the 2010-2019 decade average revised up 0.1 point to 2.1 per cent. (+4pp)

Output-gap mechanics: with CBI retail sales balances at minus 32 per cent for an eleventh consecutive month, EY warning of recession if the Strait of Hormuz blockade runs into 2027, and unemployment forecast to reach 5.3 per cent by end-2026, a downturn before 2030 is plausible. Recovery growth landing inside 2030-2039 would mechanically lift the decade mean by roughly 0.4 to 0.6 points, exactly as post-crisis reflation lifted the 2010s to a revised 2.1 per cent. (+4pp)

AI diffusion showing up in hiring and easing fiscal pressure: the Lloyds Business Barometer reported on 17 August 2026 that 54 per cent of UK firms have created AI-linked roles, and analysts now expect gilt yields to fall ahead of the 28 October Budget, potentially restoring the 10 to 12 billion pounds of headroom lost this year and reducing the risk that public capital spending is cut to meet the fiscal rules. (+3pp)
factors_down: Demographics leave productivity doing almost all the work: ONS 2024-based projections have the population rising from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million by mid-2034 with all growth from net migration; working-age population up about 0.33 per cent a year, deaths exceeding births from mid-2026, net migration at 171,000 in the year to December 2025 and projected at 138,000 in 2026, and the pensionable-age population up 14.6 per cent. Labour input contributes 0.2 to 0.5 points a year. (-8pp)

Bailey's own decomposition puts the Bank's recent-history potential growth below the bar: at Mansion House on 14 July 2026 he set post-crisis UK potential supply growth at 1.3 per cent a year, with productivity contributing only 0.4 points and labour supply 0.8 points, against 2.8 per cent pre-crisis with productivity at 2.4 points. The 2030s remove the labour-supply leg, so clearing 1.5 per cent requires the productivity contribution to more than triple from its post-crisis average. (-7pp)

The ONS's own preferred measure still shows deceleration: the 18 August 2026 productivity flash has RTI output per hour up only 0.7 per cent year on year in Q2 2026 and minus 0.8 per cent quarter on quarter after an upwardly revised plus 1.1 per cent in Q1; the LFS measure was minus 0.2 per cent year on year and just 2.3 per cent above its 2019 average, with information and communication contributing plus 2.8 per cent against 2019 while human health and social work contributed minus 0.9 per cent. (-6pp)

Investment forecasts still being marked down despite the Q2 print: the EY UK Economic Outlook of August 2026 downgrades 2026 business investment to a fall of 0.7 per cent from the zero growth projected in May, citing energy costs and inflation higher for longer, with 2027 and 2028 investment growth cut to 1.8 and 2.6 per cent and unemployment rising to 5.3 per cent by end-2026. Capital deepening is only 0.2 points of OBR potential output in 2029 and a weak late-2020s investment path erodes the 2030s capital stock. (-5pp)

The OBR medium-term anchor sits at or below the bar with a one-way revision record: November 2025 cut medium-term TFP growth from 1.1 to 0.8 per cent, taking 2029 potential output growth to 1.5 per cent, and March 2026 left TFP unchanged at 0.8 per cent by 2030. The FRS names a downside scenario in which productivity growth remains at 0.5 per cent, close to its post-financial-crisis average. The OBR's Briefing Paper No. 9 puts the AI contribution at around 0.2 points, matching Penn Wharton's early-2030s peak. (-5pp)

The foundation of the bull case may be eroding on its own terms: the ONS labour market transformation update of August 2026 reports LFS response levels for waves two to five slightly above their pre-pandemic level in January to March 2026 after incentive and interviewer interventions, with the Transformed LFS due to become the headline measure in 2027. If the survey denominator is repairing itself, the wedge that the Resolution Foundation and CEP LSE measures exploit should narrow, and the direction of that narrowing is not known. (-4pp)
key_uncertainties: Which productivity series is right. Credible estimates for the same economy over the same recent window span more than a full percentage point: minus 0.2 per cent year on year (ONS LFS), plus 0.7 per cent (ONS RTI, the official recommendation since June 2026), 1.1 per cent a year since Q3 2024 (Resolution Foundation), roughly 1.6 per cent annualised (CEP LSE OP74), 1.8 per cent private sector (Morgan Stanley). With labour input demographically capped at 0.2 to 0.5 points, essentially the entire answer sits inside that dispersion.

Whether even the optimists' number is enough. Taking the Resolution Foundation's 1.1 per cent at face value and adding 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input gives 1.3 to 1.6 per cent, centred near 1.4. The bull case as currently measured lands just short of the bar, so YES requires the pickup not merely to persist but to accelerate, or requires the CEP LSE and Morgan Stanley readings to be closer to the truth.

Whether the OBR's fifty-year baseline of around one and a half per cent real GDP growth describes the 2030s or only the later decades. TFP is still climbing towards 0.8 per cent in 2030 on the medium-term forecast, so the 2030s are the lowest slice of the long-run window; if convergence to 1.4 per cent productivity is faster than I assume, the decade mean could clear the bar on official assumptions alone.

Whether the UK has a recession before 2030 rather than inside the window. EY explicitly warns of recession if the Strait of Hormuz blockade lasts into 2027, with unemployment reaching 5.3 per cent by end-2026. Recovery inside 2030-2039 lifts the decade mean by 0.4 to 0.6 points; a recession inside the window cuts it by a similar amount. This alone makes the distribution wide and mildly bimodal.

Whether net migration settles near the ONS long-run assumption of about 230,000 a year or nearer the 138,000 projected for 2026 and the 171,000 recorded for the year to December 2025. The gap is worth roughly 0.2 to 0.3 points a year on headline GDP growth through the 2030s, a large fraction of the distance to the threshold, and it is a policy choice rather than a forecast.

Whether the OBR at the 28 October 2026 EFO leans on the new administrative-data evidence or on the weak official flash, and whether the Healey Budget's consolidation is scored as reducing potential output. Falling gilt yields may restore 10 to 12 billion pounds of headroom, but with a new Burnham government, a first Healey Budget and additional defence commitments, the political economy of that judgement is less predictable than usual.
update_triggers: Revise UP if the OBR at the 28 October 2026 Budget EFO raises, or explicitly declines to cut, its 0.8 per cent medium-term TFP assumption and cites the RTI or administrative-data evidence from the Resolution Foundation or CEP LSE in doing so, or if it brings the medium-term path closer to the 1.4 per cent long-run productivity baseline of the July 2026 Fiscal risks and sustainability report; a move back toward 1.1 per cent would be worth 5 to 8 points.

Revise UP if the ONS productivity flash for Q3 2026 on 17 November 2026 shows RTI-based output per hour back above 1.5 per cent year on year, or if the new component-based labour productivity methods article due September 2026 raises the measured level or trend, or if revised Q2 business investment on 30 September confirms two solid quarters of capital formation growth against EY's forecast fall of 0.7 per cent for the year.

Revise UP if the Bank of England lifts its potential supply estimate above 0.3 to 0.4 per cent a quarter in the November 2026 Monetary Policy Report, or explicitly revises up the 0.4 percentage point productivity contribution Bailey cited on 14 July, or if the quarterly national accounts on 30 September and the Blue Book revisions article on 30 October confirm the ONS upward reporting wedge of about plus 0.06 points a year is durable.

Revise UP if the within-sector productivity gains are replicated on ONS industry-level data showing spread beyond information and communication (plus 2.8 per cent versus 2019) into human health and social work (minus 0.9 per cent), construction and public services, following the retail evidence reported on 24 August, since those sectors are where the employment weight sits.

Revise DOWN if the OBR cuts its trend productivity assumption again on 28 October 2026 by the 0.1 to 0.2 points analysts expect, if the Budget package is scored as net contractionary for potential output, or if public capital spending is cut to meet the fiscal rules despite the expected fall in gilt yields and the extra defence commitments.

Revise DOWN if the administrative-data measures are rebutted by the ONS as the Transformed Labour Force Survey is bedded in ahead of becoming the headline measure in 2027, if the RTI-based series decelerates for a second consecutive quarter on 17 November confirming the Q2 minus 0.8 per cent fall, or if net migration settles durably below 150,000 a year and working-age population growth to 2034 is revised below 0.3 per cent a year.
